candidats.titre: Coase Meets Negishi: Property Rights, Welfare Weights, and Distributional Consequences in Climate Economics -- by Simon F. Lang, Matthew D. Gordon, Matthew J. Kotchen
candidats.resume: We develop a property-rights based approach for defining welfare weights in economic models of climate change. Whether there is a "right to pollute" or a "right to no pollution" is increasingly contested in legislatures, courts, and international climate negotiations. We show how these notions of property rights can provide the basis for "Coasean welfare weights" that are applicable in multilateral public goods settings. Distributional questions are addressed through positive analysis, conditional on property rights, rather than normative views about redistribution. The implied transfers are consistent with a bargained solution over the net benefits of addressing climate change and reflect the value of property rights over emissions. The approach defines efficient allocations that generate Pareto improvements, in contrast to commonly used Negishi weights. We implement the approach in a global integrated assessment model to quantify what countries have at stake in ongoing political and legal debates about emissions-related property rights.

candidats.titre: Governance Regimes, Economic Mobility, and the Composition of Public Investment: Evidence from the Democratization of Villages in India -- by Andrew D. Foster, Mark R. Rosenzweig
candidats.resume: We develop a quantifiable general-equilibrium model of village governance, motivated by India’s democratization, to study how political institutions shape public goods provision and economic development. The model features two groups, landowners and landless workers, with different preferences over public goods such as irrigation, schools, and employment programs. Households from both groups can enter nonfarm entrepreneurship, but face credit-dependent entry costs. We compare oligarchy, where landowners control public goods decisions, with democracy, where electoral competition determines policy based on the relative sizes of the two groups. The calibrated model predicts that democratization’s effects on public goods and growth are not uniform; they depend on population composition and the ease of occupational mobility through access to credit. Using a 37-year village-level panel from India (1971–2006) and exploiting variation in democratization driven by state and national reforms, we find strong support for these predictions. Financial intermediation shifts landless households’ preferences from wage-enhancing policies toward schooling, increasing nonfarm business entry. As a result, democracy provides fewer schools than oligarchy when credit is unavailable, but more schools when credit is accessible. We also show that transfers to the landless increase schooling under democracy but reduce it under oligarchy. These findings highlight how governance structures and economic conditions jointly determine the effectiveness of development policies.

candidats.titre: Salaire d’appoint, le « quart en moins » : l’économiste Rachel Silvera retrace un siècle d’inégalités salariales
candidats.resume: Les « munitionnettes », pendant la Première Guerre mondiale, se sont battues pour l’égalité salariale (ici, les ouvrières de l’usine Decauville à Corbeil dans l’Essonne, en 1915). Wikimediacommons Chaque automne, le hashtag lancé en 2016 par le média Les Glorieuses fixe une date symbolique : celle à partir de laquelle les femmes, compte tenu des inégalités salariales entre femmes et hommes, travaillent « gratuitement » jusqu’à la fin de l’année. Dix ans après, l’économiste Rachel Silvera remonte aux origines du « salaire d’appoint », revient sur les luttes qui ont remis en cause cette conception du travail féminin et explique pourquoi les inégalités salariales persistent. The Conversation : Comment s’est construite historiquement l’idée que le salaire d’une femme serait un revenu « d’appoint » ? Rachel Silvera : Les femmes ont toujours travaillé, comme le rappelle l’historienne Sylvie Schweitzer dans son livre qui porte ce titre, et elles ont toujours été moins payées. Leur salaire a été assimilé à un salaire d’appoint, ou complément de revenu. C’est au départ une norme sociale, dictée par le Code civil de Napoléon Iᵉʳ. L’article 213 disposait que « le mari doit protection à sa femme, la femme obéissance à son mari ». L’idée est qu’une femme n’est pas une citoyenne à part entière. Elle ne vit pas seule, car elle dépend forcément de son père ou de son mari. Derrière une femme se cache toujours un homme. Le mariage fait de cette dépendance une norme économique. Le Code civil considère d’ailleurs la femme comme une mineure en passant de la tutelle de son père à celle de son…

candidats.titre: La Francophonie, multilatéralisme des faibles ?
candidats.resume: L’ESSENTIEL L’Organisation internationale de la Francophonie estime à 396 millions le nombre de locuteurs francophones dans le monde, dont 65 % en Afrique. Aucune puissance émergente ne siège dans les rangs de l’OIF, son budget dépend de quelques bailleurs du Nord, et l’influence française recule. À quelques jours du Sommet de Phnom Penh, au Cambodge, les 15 et 16 novembre, le nombre ne fait pas la puissance. Reste à savoir si la faiblesse peut devenir une force. Les 15 et 16 novembre 2026, les chefs d’État et de gouvernement de la Francophonie se réuniront à Phnom Penh pour leur XXᵉ Sommet . Le lieu ne doit rien au hasard. Le Cambodge est le pays de Norodom Sihanouk , l’un des pères fondateurs du mouvement francophone, et l’Asie du Sud-Est n’avait plus accueilli de sommet depuis Hanoï, en 1997 . Le thème retenu, « Réinvestir dans la paix pour une prospérité partagée et une stabilité durable » , sonne comme un programme. Quatre candidats briguent le secrétariat général, dont la titulaire, Louise Mushikiwabo ; pour la première fois, ils ont été auditionnés devant la Conférence ministérielle. Les absents pèseront pourtant autant que les présents. En mars 2025, le Mali, le Burkina Faso et le Niger ont annoncé leur retrait de l’Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF). Le Niger en était un membre fondateur, et c’est à Bamako qu’avait été proclamée, en 2000, l’ indissociabilité de la démocratie et de la Francophonie . Le bouleversement de l’ordre mondial rend dès lors une question pressante : que pèse un multilatéralisme de puissances moyennes et d’États fragiles…

candidats.titre: Assiste-t-on à la fin du « privilège exorbitant » des États-Unis ?
candidats.resume: L’ESSENTIEL Depuis 1944, les États-Unis bénéficient, selon une expression de Valéry Giscard d’Estaing, d’un « privilège exorbitant » grâce au dollar en tant que première monnaie internationale. Une étude questionne ce privilège tout en anticipant sa prochaine disparition, avec des conséquences majeures sur l’économie mondiale. Car si le dollar reste encore la première monnaie internationale, l’euro ou le yuan se tiennent en embuscade. La hausse récente des taux d’intérêt aux États-Unis – les taux à 10 ans ont dépassé les 5 % la semaine du 14 septembre dernier, une première depuis la crise financière de 2008 – est-elle le signal de la fin du « privilège exorbitant » des États-Unis ? Le « privilège exorbitant » est une expression utilisée pour la première fois par Valéry Giscard d’Estaing, en 1965, pour dénoncer la position dominante du dollar dans le système de Bretton Woods. Elle désigne l’avantage unique dont bénéficient les États-Unis grâce à l’utilisation internationale de leur monnaie. À cette époque, le dollar est la seule monnaie convertible en or et les autres monnaies nationales doivent fixer leur parité par rapport au dollar – ce que l’on appelle des taux de change fixe. Le dollar, monnaie internationale par excellence, conférait aux États-Unis un avantage considérable ; ils pouvaient financer leur déficit commercial dans leur propre devise, ce qui leur permettait d’avoir un déficit « sans pleurs », selon l’expression de Jacques Rueff, ancien ministre d’État. Cependant, la fin du système de Bretton Woods n’a pas mis un terme à la domination du dollar, bien au…

candidats.titre: Midterms 2026 : le populisme à l'épreuve de la démocratie
candidats.resume: Les élections de mi-mandat se sont soldées par un sérieux revers pour le parti républicain. La politologue Élisa Chelle, auteure de La démocratie à l'épreuve du populisme : les leçons du trumpisme (Odile Jacob, 2025), analyse les recompositions ayant contribué à cette victoire démocrate, ainsi que les limites du populisme au sein même de la démocratie américaine. The Conversation : Ces midterms peuvent-elles être considérées comme un référendum anti-Trump ? Élisa Chelle : En partie, oui. Les enquêtes montrent que 40 à 50 % des électeurs se sont déplacés avant tout pour voter contre Donald Trump. Une proportion à peu près équivalente a voté indépendamment de lui, tandis que le reste s'est plutôt mobilisé pour le soutenir. Cette dimension anti-Trump s'est aussi traduite par une participation inhabituelle pour des élections de mi-mandat : 49,4 %, contre 30 à 40 % habituellement. Il y a donc eu une mobilisation supplémentaire dans les urnes, notamment à travers le vote anticipé, qui a bénéficié aux démocrates. Six millions de leurs électeurs avaient boudé les bureaux de vote à la présidentielle de 2024. Le style de Trump et la conjoncture actuelle les ont remobilisés. Pour Trump, cette défaite est d'autant plus coûteuse qu'il avait personnellement placé ces élections sur le terrain plébiscitaire. Il avait fait de sa victoire de 2024 dans les six États pivots qu'il avait perdus en 2020 un véritable titre de légitimité. candidats.titre: Les centres de données créent-ils vraiment des emplois ? Ce que révèle l’étude de 1 584 sites
candidats.resume: L’ESSENTIEL Aux États-Unis, l’ouverture d’un centre de données s’accompagne en moyenne de 1 000 à 1 300 emplois locaux supplémentaires hors construction. Dans les comtés américains étudiés, ces emplois mettent trois à cinq ans à apparaître et relèvent surtout des secteurs au service des data centers. À l’inverse, l’étude ne trouve guère de hausse d’emploi dans la restauration, le commerce et les services de proximité. Construire un data center exige des investissements colossaux : terrain, bâtiments, matériel informatique et infrastructures électriques. Pourtant, une fois en service, ces installations n’emploient en général que quelques dizaines de personnes , par exemple des techniciens informatiques, des ingénieurs ou des agents de sécurité. Alors que des milliards de dollars sont investis dans de nouveaux data centers partout aux États-Unis, les territoires concernés se demandent ce qu’ils y gagneront . Ce scepticisme quant aux retombées locales nourrit une opposition croissante à leur construction , de l’Ohio au Texas . Cette fronde a contribué à retarder ou à faire annuler des projets de data centers d’une valeur de 156 milliards de dollars (environ 139 milliards d’euros) rien qu’en 2025. Nous sommes enseignants-chercheurs spécialistes de l’immobilier et de l’ économie urbaine , et nous étudions notamment la façon dont les grands investissements réalisés dans un territoire façonnent son économie. Nous avons donc voulu répondre à une question au cœur de ces conflits : les data centers créent-ils réellement des emplois là où ils sont construits ? Pour le savoir, nous…

candidats.titre: Incendie de Limoges : de l’« émeutier » au « terroriste », comment les mots construisent une menace politique
candidats.resume: L’ESSENTIEL Nommer ne consiste pas seulement à identifier, mais aussi à adopter un point de vue. Comment les désignations successives des auteurs présumés de l’incendie de Limoges, le 17 octobre 2026, ont-elles orienté la lecture des faits ? L’analyse d’un corpus de discours médiatiques permet d’interroger les processus de circulation et de transformation des discours publics. « Hordes de sauvages » , « base arrière » , « camps d’entraînement terroristes » : depuis l’incendie de l’hôtel de ville de Limoges, survenu le 17 octobre 2026 en marge de mobilisations sociales, les désignations des auteurs présumés des violences et les accusations concernant leur organisation se multiplient. Plusieurs responsables politiques mettent en cause l’ultragauche et désignent le plateau de Millevaches , territoire rural du Limousin, comme un possible lieu de repli ou de préparation des violences. À partir de déclarations publiques et d’articles de presse publiés entre le 17 et le 27 octobre, observons comment les mots employés et leur circulation contribuent à transformer un événement local en symbole d’une menace politique plus générale. Nommer les violences, désigner leurs auteurs « Émeutiers », « casseurs », « assaillants », « militants d’ultragauche » : ces désignations ne sont pas interchangeables. Les trois premières renvoient aux actes ou aux rôles attribués aux protagonistes ; la dernière introduit une appartenance politique, réelle ou supposée. candidats.titre: Que disent les données de la réalité de la mondialisation et de son évolution ?
candidats.resume: L’ESSENTIEL La mondialisation apparaît comme une évidence, qu’on s’en réjouisse ou qu’on le critique. Les débats sur le sujet s’appuient rarement sur les données publiées qui laissent voir une réalité plus nuancée et plus contrastée que bien des jugements à l’emporte-pièce. À l’heure où la démondialisation est évoquée, il est essentiel de s’appuyer sur des données fiables, observées sur une certaine durée. Pour sortir des impressions plus ou moins fondées. On débat beaucoup de la mondialisation, de ses effets, de ses dégâts, de sa responsabilité dans le trumpisme ou le Brexit, ou de la fin de la mondialisation, qu’elle soit attendue ou crainte. Et ce depuis trois décennies ! En effet, dès le milieu des années 1990, on a pu chercher à l’accuser de beaucoup de maux, on a pu chercher à la défendre, ou à la réorienter, et, depuis, à intervalles réguliers, se rejoue ce affrontement. Or l’une des caractéristiques de ces débats est d’avoir souvent entretenu des rapports difficiles avec les données. Un bon exemple est celui du livre à succès de Thomas Friedman, The World is Flat , qui constitue l’une des descriptions les plus tonitruantes de la mondialisation, présentée comme un vaste aplatissement du monde, unifié dorénavant dans tous ses cantons par des circulations de biens, de personnes, de marchandises et d’informations que plus rien n’arrête. Cet ouvrage fourmillait de descriptions hautes en couleur, de perspectives audacieuses et d’intuitions brillantes, mais – et c’est un problème quand il s’agit de parler d’un processus qu’on présente comme nouveau et radicalement…

candidats.titre: En Inde, la Gen Z des « cafards » invoque la Constitution et l’héritage d’Ambedkar
candidats.resume: L’ESSENTIEL Né au printemps 2026 d’une remarque méprisante du président de la Cour suprême, le mouvement des « cafards » est passé en quelques semaines de la satire numérique à la rue. Après avoir obtenu la démission du ministre de l’éducation, il s’est engagé dans une nouvelle bataille autour du droit de vote. Derrière les masques de cafards apparaît surtout une jeunesse qui réinvestit le drapeau indien, la Constitution et la figure de son architecte B. R. Ambedkar pour contester le pouvoir au nom même de la nation. À Jantar Mantar, au cœur de New Delhi, Sagar ne correspond guère à l’image répandue de l’étudiant contestataire issu des classes moyennes urbaines. Originaire du district très majoritairement rural de Satara, dans l’État du Maharashtra, il a terminé ses études universitaires et préparé des concours de recrutement public. Pourtant, m’explique-t-il en cet été 2026, il a se retrouve à faire un travail manuel et estime que « le gouvernement en est le seul responsable. » Les fuites de sujets, les examens reportés, les limites d’âge qui se rapprochent, les emplois qui se dérobent : autant de bouleversements qui n’ont rien, à ses yeux, de simples dysfonctionnements administratifs. Ils compromettent le calendrier d’une vie entière : trouver un travail, se marier, soutenir sa famille, accéder enfin à un statut social. Sagar appartient à cette mobilisation improbable qui s’est baptisée Cockroach Janta Party, le « Parti populaire des cafards ». Malgré son nom, le CJP n’est pas, à ce jour, un parti politique au sens classique, mais un mouvement né d’une insulte retournée…

a8.texte:
The gap between open and closed AI models in cyber capabilities keeps shrinking
AI agents can break into realistic corporate networks on their own, Vals AI finds
The Vals CyberOffense benchmark simulates realistic corporate networks to test this. Each agent operates solo on an isolated attack machine, starting with nothing but a public web address and zero human help.
GPT-6 Sol, part of OpenAI's restricted Daybreak cyber program, posted the best result at 80.8 percent of objectives. Deepseek V4.1 Flash 1017, a freely available open-weight model, isn't far behind at 72.8 percent and costs only about $3 per run instead of roughly $22. Once a model's weights are public, no provider can control or restrict how it's used, Vals researchers say.
In the harder Lighthouse test, Daybreak took over admin control of the first company, stole passwords, and used them to break into the second company. It completed 27 of 31 objectives in under three hours. Deepseek managed 21 objectives at a tenth of the cost and wasn't limited solely by safety guardrails.
Longer runtimes turned out to be critical as well. Deepseek scored zero results in its first 25 million tokens and made most of its progress only after 100 million tokens. Short tests therefore underestimate the real potential of open models.
Vals points out that the same findings create an opportunity for defenders, because the very models that exploit vulnerabilities can help companies find and fix them first. Attacks on real networks are likely to increase in the coming months, according to Vals.
Open models close the gap fast, earlier studies confirm
The results align with a recent analysis by the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI) from July. The gap between open and closed frontier models in cyber capabilities has shrunk to four to seven months. For most of 2025, that gap still stood at six to ten months.
Open models are also much cheaper. A cyber-range run with Deepseek V4-Pro costs just $1.19 according to AISI, compared with $85 for Anthropic's Opus 4.5. The safety measures on the open models proved largely ineffective.
A recent study by Anthropic also showed that the freely available model GLM-5-3 can build exploits at nearly the same level as the internal top model Mythos.

AI auditors catch most agent misbehavior but flood reviewers with false alarms, new study finds
AI models can often spot problematic behavior by other AI agents in logs. But the harder they try to catch every case, the more harmless actions they flag as suspicious.
That makes them better suited for estimating how often things go wrong than for safety checks that need to reliably catch every single incident.
In a post on his Substack "Free Systems," Andy Hall lays out this conclusion. Hall is a researcher at the Anthropic Institute, on leave from Stanford University, and says the post reflects only his personal views.
Hall replicated and extended a study by the research organization METR. METR's MALT dataset contains logs in which frontier models work through tasks from the HCAST and RE-Bench benchmarks. Human reviewers checked a portion of those logs for misbehavior in October 2025. Hall wanted to know whether AI models could find the same cases, so he tested GPT-5 and GPT-5 nano, both already examined by METR, along with the newer GPT-6 Astra, Opus 4.8, and Gemini 3.8 Flash.
The analysis compares the models at a false-alarm rate of 5 percent: out of 100 clean logs, five are wrongly flagged as suspicious on average. At that threshold, GPT-5 caught nearly 98 percent of reward hacking cases—instances where an agent passes a task through tricks instead of a genuine solution. Gemini 3.8 Flash found barely half.
In sandbagging, a model deliberately makes its abilities appear weaker, for example by solving tasks poorly on purpose to dodge an evaluation or restriction. All auditors caught between 71 and 81 percent of these cases. The sandbagging cases are mostly synthetic, however: METR's researchers instructed models to sabotage and then removed those instructions from the visible chain-of-thought logs.
Every auditor caught the clear-cut cases. OpenAI's o3, for instance, was supposed to solve a programming task in Rust. The model noticed it shared a code library with the evaluation system and rewrote the scoring function so that every submission counted as correct. All auditor models classified this as reward hacking, just as the human reviewers did.
Subtler cases slipped through. Claude Sonnet 4 used a numerical condition in its code that was explicitly forbidden. No auditor flagged it as cheating; GPT-6 Astra charitably called it an implementation bug.
Newer models barely reduce false alarms
Newer and more expensive models were not consistently better auditors. Hall plotted the results against API costs, which he uses as a proxy for how current and capable a model is. GPT-5 beat GPT-6 Astra on reward hacking by a wide margin, even though it costs only about an eighth as much per 1,000 logs.
GPT-5 detected sandbagging about as well as GPT-6 Astra and Opus 4.8. Opus 4.8's weak showing on reward hacking could hint at self-favoritism, according to Hall, because the logs mostly come from Claude—but he says that cannot be proven. Across his comparison, there is no clear progress in bringing down false-alarm rates. Combining multiple models did not clearly improve results either.
When auditors are tuned to an 80 percent detection rate, the best models reach false-alarm rates of 2.5 to 3 percent on both reward hacking and sandbagging. Some models do far worse: to catch 80 percent of reward-hacking cases, Opus 4.8 flagged 40 percent and Gemini 3.8 Flash flagged 63 percent of harmless logs as suspicious.
In Hall's worked example with 100,000 agent sessions per month, a 3 percent false-alarm rate would produce nearly 3,000 false warnings against roughly 2,000 real hits. He fears human reviewers facing such stacks would eventually go numb and wave through genuine cases.
A second test using the R-Judge dataset from Shanghai Jiao Tong University shows a similar trade-off for everyday agent tasks. At 5 percent false alarms, Opus 4.8 caught almost 96 percent of unsafe actions. When auditors need to find 95 percent, nearly all models stay below 10 percent false alarms, with Gemini 3.8 Flash even under 4 percent. But when the required detection rate jumps to 99 percent, the false-alarm rate climbs to 15 percent even for the best model, GPT-6 Astra. Gemini 3.8 Flash—the leader at the 95 percent threshold—then flagged 81 percent of safe actions as unsafe.
Large agent incidents overwhelm manual review
The Hugging Face incident shows how pressing the question is. A swarm of OpenAI agents left behind roughly 1,300 transcripts and 1.2 million file fragments. METR analyzed the data largely with AI agents, spending API credits worth about $400,000. The analysis used GPT-5.6 Sol, among other models, which, as previously reported, was itself one of the models involved in the incident.
METR acknowledged that the model often uncritically adopted the perspective of the agents it was examining and that the investigation was not robust against potential deception by the analysis agents. METR has since called for serious incidents to be investigated systematically and as independently as possible.
Whether AI auditors go easy on their own maker's models is still open
Hall's study has its own limits. It is a pilot. For comparability, he kept METR's original prompt largely unchanged; Fable 5 and Opus 5 refused to run the evaluation entirely under that prompt. The reward-hacking numbers rest on just 47 cases, so a single case shifts the rate by about two percentage points. Whether models evaluate agents from the same maker fairly is something Hall says he still wants to investigate.
He calls for auditor models with far fewer false alarms. He also says it needs to be clarified who bears responsibility for which kinds of agent misbehavior. Hall discusses a proposal to give users more control over their own AI auditors.
Some of that is already possible, he notes: coding agents like Codex and Claude Code let users specify that certain actions can run without asking for approval. Anyone who grants such permissions should, in return, bear more responsibility for the consequences. A world where AI can only be checked by other AI would be strange and could get expensive, Hall writes.

À l’occasion de la présentation de la nouvelle édition de L’Avenir en commun, samedi 7 novembre, La France insoumise a transformé le Bourget en théâtre de campagne. Scénographie immersive, démonstration de force militante et discours de Jean-Luc Mélenchon résolument tourné vers la jeunesse, le mouvement entend faire de son programme le premier acte de la présidentielle de 2027. Reportage
Mobilisation de la jeunesse : « Nous avons construit un État-providence qui fonctionne seulement pour les adultes », reconnaît cette eurodéputée
Comme une traînée de poudre, ces dernières semaines, une multitude de mouvements sociaux se sont propagés à travers le continent. Parfois accompagnés de scènes de violence spectaculaires et de heurts, ils présentent aussi des similitudes de fond. En Italie, l’ampleur des manifestations, qui ont rassemblé de 250 000 à plus d’un million de personnes selon les sources, a pris de court le gouvernement Meloni. En France, le mouvement, parti d’une colère lycéenne, a pris de l’ampleur au fil des semaines jusqu’à atteindre 1,6 million de manifestants ce 5 novembre, jour de grève générale, selon les chiffres des syndicats (575 000 selon le ministère).
Une convergence des luttes transfrontalières ?
Malgré la diversité des contextes nationaux, la contestation s’articule autour de revendications partagées et d’une solidarité transfrontalière. « Ce sont des mots d’ordre qui traversent toute l’Europe, parce que c’est une situation finalement similaire, et donc avec une jeunesse qui se reconnaît dans les mouvements les uns des autres, avec une solidarité qui est très belle aussi », s’enthousiasme l’eurodéputée Emma Fourreau (France, La Gauche). Pour cette élue de La France insoumise, le mot d’ordre de la jeunesse européenne est bien commun : « C’est la défense du droit à l’avenir, à la fois des jeunes et des peuples en général, parce que ce sont les mêmes causes qui frappent partout en Europe : la crise du logement, le coût de la vie et le délabrement de l’éducation. » L’élue pointe du doigt des classes surchargées, un manque chronique de professeurs et des infrastructures scolaires dégradées, illustrées par des situations d’insalubrité dans les établissements.
Modèle social en crise et inflation
Derrière cette colère, certains élus lisent une remise en cause des promesses non tenues de la démocratie libérale. C’est le cas de l’Italienne Elisabetta Gualmini : « [Les jeunes manifestants] veulent le capitalisme que les générations précédentes ont vécu », analyse l’eurodéputée (Renew Europe). Selon elle, la nouvelle génération fait face à un paradoxe intenable : on lui enjoint de s’investir et de se former, sans pour autant lui octroyer les conditions matérielles de son émancipation. « Nous avons construit un État-providence qui fonctionne seulement pour les adultes, pour les insiders, et pas pour les jeunes », regrette-t-elle. « En Italie, chaque personne qui naît a six grands-parents sur les épaules. »
Cette fracture générationnelle se superpose à une crise économique alimentée par une inflation persistante, s’établissant en moyenne à 3,8 % dans l’Union européenne, avec des pics à 4,2 % en Italie, 4,5 % en Belgique et jusqu’à 6,5 % en Roumanie. Pour l’eurodéputée belge Assita Kanko (N-VA/ECR), la solution ne réside pas dans un endettement ou des dépenses publiques incontrôlées, mais dans la relance de la compétitivité et du tissu productif, en s’inspirant notamment des recommandations du rapport Draghi. « L’État-providence est en train de s’effondrer parce que, dans beaucoup de pays, il y a des gens qui profitent du système sans contribuer », dénonce-t-elle. « On ne peut pas dépenser, dépenser, dépenser sans créer de la valeur et de la prospérité durable. »
Réponse politique ou sécuritaire ?
La réponse politique à ces contestations interroge et divise les États membres de l’Union. En Italie, elle s’est traduite par une fermeté accrue et près de 600 arrestations. Face aux pillages, la présidente du Conseil, Giorgia Meloni, a même eu recours à l’armée. L’eurodéputée Elisabetta Gualmini, tout en condamnant fermement les actes de vandalisme et les violences, insiste sur le fait qu’une logique purement sécuritaire est vouée à l’échec. « Il faut penser à des mesures concrètes pour les jeunes », plaide cette élue Renew. Elle appelle ainsi à l’intégration immédiate d’une évaluation d’impact intergénérationnel dans les politiques publiques européennes.
Sur le volet sécuritaire, la question du maintien de l’ordre suscite de vifs débats. Assita Kanko, pour le groupe des Réformistes et Conservateurs européens, situé à la droite de l’hémicycle du Parlement européen, dénonce avec force les agressions répétées subies par les forces de police, qu’elle érige en garantes de l’autorité républicaine face aux casseurs. Pour elle, ces derniers sont l’expression d’une crise de l’éducation au sens moral et d’une « société où il n’y a plus de responsabilités ». L’eurodéputée belge critique en outre l’attitude de la gauche radicale, qu’elle accuse d’entretenir un climat d’impunité et d’avoir « infiltré » les manifestants. À l’inverse, l’insoumise Emma Fourreau rejette une telle lecture, fustigeant une « dénonciation à géométrie variable » et dénonçant une « violence policière » qu’elle juge disproportionnée. Elle justifie sa présence aux manifestations en France, comme celle du leader de La France insoumise Jean-Luc Mélenchon : « Notre place est toujours du côté de ceux qui manifestent pour leur dignité dans la vie. »
Quelle réponse politique ?
Au-delà de ces divergences idéologiques, un consensus émerge sur l’urgence d’investir dans le secteur de l’éducation. Qu’il s’agisse de l’Allemagne, confrontée à la plus grande pénurie d’enseignants à l’échelle européenne, ou de l’Italie et de la France, la revalorisation de la profession enseignante et l’amélioration des conditions d’apprentissage apparaissent désormais comme des leviers pour désamorcer la crise et redonner des perspectives à la jeunesse.
« Le problème, c’est que [les enseignants] sont vraiment très peu payés », déplore Elisabetta Gualmini. « On ne peut pas prétendre que les enseignants soient présents et aillent dans les écoles, qu’ils se déplacent d’une région à l’autre, sans les payer plus et donc il faut donner une valeur sociale plus haute aux enseignants », conclut l’eurodéputée italienne, dans des débats qui rappellent ceux qui existent en France.

A contre-courant de la rhétorique politique dominante en France et en Europe, le député socialiste de la Drôme Paul Christophle s’apprête à défendre une proposition de loi visant à régulariser des travailleurs sans-papiers. Elle sera débattue lors de la niche parlementaire du Parti socialiste (PS) à l’Assemblée nationale, lundi 9 novembre devant la commission des lois, puis en séance, le 19 novembre.
Dans le détail, le texte prévoit de régulariser tout étranger qui justifierait de l’occupation d’une activité professionnelle en France d’une durée d’au moins six mois au cours des deux dernières années. « Ceci se traduirait par la régularisation immédiate d’environ 300 000 travailleurs sans‑papiers », estime l’élu socialiste. Ils se verraient délivrer « de plein droit » une carte de séjour portant la mention « salarié ». Une régularisation d’ampleur qui a reçu, précise le député, le soutien du candidat du PS et de Place publique à la présidentielle, Raphaël Glucksmann.
Cette proposition s’inspire directement du vaste plan de régularisation d’environ 500 000 travailleurs sans‑papiers, adopté en Espagne par le gouvernement socialiste de Pedro Sánchez, en avril. « En France, les 300 000 à 400 000 travailleurs sans‑papiers jouent un rôle indispensable dans l’économie et la vie sociale de notre pays, justifie Paul Christophle. Ils sont en première ligne, autour de nous, dans les cuisines des restaurants, les petits commerces du coin de la rue, dans le BTP, l’aide à la personne et les Ehpad ou dans les bateaux des pêcheurs en Bretagne. Ils occupent des métiers difficiles qui n’auraient pas trouvé preneur autrement. »

Six ans plus tard, c’est une affaire emblématique des violences policières qui arrive devant la cour criminelle de Paris. Lundi 9 novembre, et pour deux semaines, des magistrats jugeront Aurélien L., 29 ans, Pierre P., 37 ans et Philippe T., 50 ans, trois policiers accusés d’avoir, le 21 novembre 2020, violenté Michel Zecler dans son studio de musique, et menti sur procès-verbal pour maquiller ces violences.
Ce procès constitue l’épilogue d’un long parcours judiciaire, marqué dès ses premiers jours par la forte médiatisation des violences subies par le producteur de musique, aujourd’hui âgé de 47 ans. « Les images que nous avons tous vues de l’agression de Michel Zecler sont inacceptables. Elles nous font honte », écrivait le président de la République, Emmanuel Macron, sur Facebook, une semaine après ce passage à tabac. Cette affaire est devenue le symbole d’une mutation dans les procédures pour violences policières, dans lesquelles la preuve visuelle prend une place croissante.
Pour Michel Zecler, c’est d’une caméra de vidéosurveillance qu’est venu le salut. Car c’est dans le huis clos de son studio d’enregistrement, dans le 17e arrondissement de Paris, que s’est déroulée la scène. Ce 21 novembre 2020, le producteur pousse la porte de ses locaux, et est immédiatement suivi par un policier en civil, puis deux collègues en uniforme. Ceux-ci expliqueront avoir voulu le contrôler après l’avoir repéré dans la rue sans masque chirurgical, dont le port était alors obligatoire, en pleine pandémie de Covid-19.

L’accident s’est produit vers 7 h 30 sur la départementale D22 à Lent, au sud de Bourg-en-Bresse. Le car, affrété par la région Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, transportait 49 personnes, dont 23 mineurs. Il avait déclaré aux enquêteurs qu’il circulait avec le régulateur de vitesse et respectait la limitation fixée à 70 kilomètres à l’heure. « Cet élément devra également faire l’objet de vérifications », avait souligné la procureure.
Le chauffeur avait déjà été contrôlé négatif lors d’un contrôle inopiné à la mi-octobre, et son entreprise avait fait l’objet de 106 contrôles depuis 2024, selon le ministre des transports, Philippe Tabarot, qui s’est rendu sur les lieux vendredi.

Europe to join U.S.-brokered Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, defying Kremlin objections
European officials will turn up for the U.S.-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in the United Arab Emirates this week, France's foreign minister said Sunday, days after the Kremlin had insisted there could be no role for European powers at the meeting.
"France will be there and will ensure that Europe's voice is heard," Jean-Noël Barrot told French radio. He did not say who would represent Paris, or whether French or other European officials would take part directly in negotiations, or simply observe.
The meetings, which are set to take place in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday, had previously been presented as a three-way session between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv.
The Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov had earlier ruled out a European role, saying the trilateral format had already been agreed.
Talking to a Russian news channel on Friday, he accused European governments of failing to decide who speaks for them, while acknowledging that security talks would at some point require Europe's involvement.
On Thursday, President Trump met Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev and said a coming agreement was "going to involve more than Ukraine," adding he could even say it "might involve all of Europe."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told CNN on Friday that he had not been given details of the agreement Trump had referenced, and warned: "For me, it's not simple, and it can be dangerous." He invoked the 1945 Yalta conference, where Allied leaders settled Europe's division without the involvement of several affected countries.
A stalled process restarts
This will be the fourth round of talks between the two warring nations brokered by the Trump administration, and the first since those in Geneva this February. Earlier U.S.-brokered meetings have made little progress, and the chances of a breakthrough have been reduced as the Trump administration focused on its war with Iran.
Moscow confirmed it would return to the negotiating table only following a visit by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg in October. Those talks saw Putin announce the release of an American prisoner from a Russian jail — an apparent Kremlin gesture to President Trump's earlier lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel exports. Ukraine was vehemently opposed to the fuel sales — arguing they helped replenish Moscow's war chest.
Witkoff has said the agenda for these latest talks will include postwar security arrangements and de-escalation of the conflict and humanitarian issues, shortly after Melania Trump helped broker a limited ceasefire that allowed humanitarian aid to enter a town inside Russian-occupied Ukraine.
Russia's delegation will again be led by Vladimir Medinsky, a hardline Putin aide who has participated in most talks with Ukraine since the unsuccessful first set of discussions all the way back in March 2022.
For the first time, these talks will also include Deputy Foreign Ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, as well as Yury Zhigarlovsky, a deputy head of the General Staff's operations directorate, alongside military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov.
This more senior lineup could indicate that Moscow is readier than before to address thorny political and military questions. But the U.S. think tankInstitute for the Study of War suggested some of those same Russian officials have in fact previously sought to slow down previous talks or push harder on Moscow's demands.
The gaps between the two countries remain substantial. Russia has demanded that Ukraine give up large parts of its territory and renounce NATO membership. Zelenskyy has repeatedly insisted any security commitments should be clearly spelled out, including who would act, and how, if Russia attacked again.
Skepticism and shifting politics
Some analysts expect little. In an op-ed for the Atlantic Council think tank, the former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine John Herbst argued that Putin had rejected every U.S. proposal Kyiv accepted and preferred participating in peace talks than pursuing actual peace. "Perhaps the only outcome of the talks," he wrote, "will be to agree to another round."
The meetings in the United Arab Emirates also follow Democrats' midterm victories, which Zelenskyy said could improve Ukraine's chances of more U.S. aid.
Russia, too, may be looking to push for the Trump administration's outlines of a Ukraine deal — before a Democratic-controlled Congress arrives come January.
Also hovering over the talks — the prospect of Trump, Xi, and Putin gathering for a trilateral meeting at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China later this month. While details remain murky, all sides have confirmed discussions are underway.
And as officials travel to Abu Dhabi to talk peace, the war has raged on regardless.
Zelenskyy said Russia fired 36 ballistic missiles at the Kyiv area overnight Saturday, with only four intercepted, accusing Moscow of treating diplomacy "as a form of aggression."
In southern Ukraine, the death toll from a guided-bomb strike Monday on an aid distribution site in Komyshuvakha rose to at least 55.

The life Vasilij Kovacs knew ended with a bang. It was late afternoon on March 1, 2025, when an armored vehicle smashed through the metal gate of the old farmhouse where he lived southeast of the Latvian capital, Riga.
Masked men emerged with their guns drawn. They belonged to Latvia’s State Security Service, the country’s counterintelligence agency. The officers searched the property, seizing several mobile phones, SIM cards and documents, along with a pistol with its serial number filed off, a bayonet from an AK-47 and a cellphone jammer, according to a search report later filed by the authorities. They arrested Kovacs, a Ukrainian man in his 60s who has lived in Latvia for more than 30 years.
In March, Kovacs was transferred to stand trial in Lithuania, where he is accused of planning terrorist attacks, alongside four alleged accomplices. Five others face trial in Warsaw. Lithuanian and Polish prosecutors accuse the ten men of planning and carrying out arson attacks involving cargo parcels across several European countries on behalf of Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU.
One of those incidents made headlines across Germany. In the early hours of July 20, 2024, a parcel caught fire at Leipzig Airport just before it was due to be loaded onto a DHL cargo plane. The flames engulfed an airfreight container. It was probably only because the aircraft was delayed that the fire did not break out on board.
All ten men say they did not knowingly work for Russian intelligence and say they are innocent of the terrorism charges. According to investigative files from the Office of the Prosecutor General of Lithuania, Kovacs is an example of an increasingly common category of Russian intelligence asset — the kind Western intelligence agencies call “low-level agents,” or, more tellingly, disposable agents.
The 63-year-old Ukrainian national is alleged to have been a small cog in a much larger machine. Investigators say he transported massage pillows modified to be able to conceal incendiary devices from Latvia to Lithuania.
With its own officers finding it harder to operate in Europe since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the GRU increasingly relies on intermediaries to recruit people through messaging services such as Telegram, according to investigative files from Lithuania’s State Security Department obtained by the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, of which POLITICO is a part of.
Often motivated by money, these disposable agents carry out individual assignments: Take a photograph. Mail a parcel. Move something from A to B. Sometimes the tasks are far more dangerous. Recruits may know little about the wider operation. Anyone who gets caught can be replaced.
Much has been written about these agents and the shadow war unfolding across Europe. But one perspective is usually missing: Who are these people? How did they become pawns in a new Cold War that is growing increasingly hot? Are they simply perpetrators — or are they victims, too?
For this article, we spoke to Kovacs several times, interviewed his daughter and examined thousands of pages of investigative records. Together, they reveal a sabotage network where meticulous intelligence planning goes hand in hand with human incompetence, and in which ordinary people are, well, disposable.
The GRU, contacted through the Russian government’s Press Service, did not reply to a request for comment.
The courier
The entrance to the prison where Kovacs has been held on remand for more than a year sits beneath a rusting metal roof. A Lithuanian investigating judge has authorized us to interview him, but when we arrive in September 2026, prison officers refuse to let us in. We need a separate document from the prison administration, they explain. We submit the additional paperwork but eventually have to leave.
A few days later, Kovacs calls from prison. He is allowed around 20 minutes on the phone each day, time he usually reserves for his family. But over the following weeks, he calls us repeatedly. “I also want to know how I ended up in here,” he says. He insists this is about justice, not himself. “I don’t value my own life particularly highly,” he says. “I’m not going to tell you how many times people have tried to kill me.”
There’s a lot about what Kovacs says during our conversations that’s unclear. But on one point, at least, his account and the investigators’ findings agree: He transported a package. Where they disagree is whether he knew what was inside it, what it was intended for — and who was behind the operation.
According to the Lithuanian investigative files, Kovacs’ involvement in the affair began on June 27, 2024, when someone contacted him on Telegram with a request.
He barely knew the man, but the two had been introduced by a mutual friend: Andrei Baburov, a former Russian submarine commander who was also the godfather of Kovacs’ 11-year-old son. The two men had met through their shared passion for the sea. Kovacs is a sailor who occasionally earns money delivering yachts for their owners. He says he first met Baburov while transporting a yacht between St. Petersburg and the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.
The request sounded harmless. A courier had fallen ill, and Kovacs was asked to collect a package and take it urgently to Vilnius, nearly four hours away by car. He agreed, collecting the package from a locker outside a supermarket in Riga using a code sent to him on Telegram by the man Baburov had introduced him to. He insists he was not paid. “If I’m helping someone I know, I do it for free,” he says.
That same day, he drove to Vilnius with his nephew. His contact on Telegram directed him to an underground parking garage. Kovacs parked outside, left the vehicle unlocked and walked away with his nephew. When they returned, the package had disappeared from the trunk. Kovacs says he had gone to buy a charging cable for his phone.
For Kovacs, that part of the job was done. But for the operation investigators have attributed to the GRU, things were only just getting started.
Burning parcels
Lithuanian investigators overseen by the Office of the Prosecutor General have reconstructed the movements of the devices used for the operation in painstaking detail, questioning witnesses and suspects, reviewing surveillance footage and digital evidence and analyzing DNA traces. The resulting files from the criminal investigation, compiling information from agencies in Lithuania, Latvia, Poland, Estonia, the U.K. and Germany, run at around 8,000 pages. They reveal a convoluted journey through the Baltic states, involving a succession of intermediaries, missed connections and improvised plans.
The man believed by Polish and Lithuanian investigators to have collected the package from Kovacs’ car was another Ukrainian, a trained chef who had spent five years in a Russian penal colony after being convicted of rape. By the summer of 2024, he was living in Poland and receiving instructions through Telegram from a handler who promised him €4,000 a month.
The following day, the chef allegedly took the massage pillows to a holiday apartment rented under a false name. He also had tubes of cosmetics filled with potentially explosive nitromethane. A video filmed inside the Airbnb apartment and later found on a suspect’s phone shows four boxes containing the massage devices and cosmetic products.
According to the Lithuanian investigative files, another intermediary was supposed to come and get the devices but could not find the entrance to the apartment complex. The chef’s handler changed the plan and ordered him to activate the ignition devices himself. The chef refused, according to an indictment filed by Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office, obtained by the Global Reporters Network. The operation had to be reorganized.
Over the following days, the boxes passed through several more hands. At one point, Lithuanian investigators lost track of them altogether. They suspected they might have traveled through Moldova. On July 13, 2024, they resurfaced in Riga, where Kovacs was drawn into the operation for a second time.
Once again, according to his account, Kovacs received a Telegram call from the acquaintance he barely knew. This time, he said, he thought he could hear Baburov in the background. He was asked to transport another shipment to Lithuania, described as “high-quality massage pillows.” On July 17, he drove to Vilnius with his nephew.
There, another man collected his package and drove it to Kaunas, where on July 18 a Ukrainian who had traveled from Poland to Lithuania retrieved it. He, too, had a criminal past, having been convicted in Poland of cyber fraud and money laundering. His instructions came from a Telegram contact calling himself “Warrior.”
The Ukrainian packed four parcels containing the massage devices, tubes of potentially explosive cosmetics and various sex toys investigators believe were included as a distraction. He activated a timer and handed the parcels to the man who had previously failed to find the entrance to the holiday apartment. That afternoon, the man dropped off two parcels at a DHL office in Vilnius. They were addressed to Wimbledon in London and to Birmingham.
At 3:17 a.m. on July 20, customs officers in Leipzig inspected the parcel bound for London. They found nothing suspicious. The parcel was due to be loaded onto a plane to London. But at 5:45 a.m., it burst into flames while still on the ground. An expert report commissioned by Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office, dated August 30, 2024, offered a terse assessment: “Fire caused by deliberate action: plausible.”
Two days later, the second parcel caught fire in a warehouse in Birmingham. That shipment, too, had previously been inspected by customs officers in Leipzig. They had found nothing.
The Ukrainian man also sent two other parcels to Poland through the DPD shipping service. In the early hours of July 21, one of them burst into flames inside a truck near Warsaw. Polish investigators recovered the other intact.
The Kremlin’s recruits
For investigators, the parcel operation is a case study in how Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU, now organizes its operations in Europe. “The July 2024 incident fully corresponds to the modus operandi favored by the GRU in recent years when planning and conducting operations,” according to a report by Lithuania’s State Security Department, also known as the VSD, obtained by the Global Reporters Network.
For years, the GRU sent its own officers abroad to carry out covert operations. But that became increasingly difficult after the failed assassination attempt against former Russian double agent Sergei Skripal in Britain in 2018 and Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine four years later. Now, the GRU leaves the dangerous work to others, increasingly relying on recruits directed through multiple layers of intermediaries.
At the top of the chain are still Russian intelligence officers. The Lithuanian report identifies Denis Smolyaninov, who, according to a decision to sanction him by the Council of the European Union, recruited operatives for sabotage missions in Europe through social media. The VSD considered it highly likely that Smolyaninov and two other GRU officers were involved in the parcel operation. Smolyaninov did not reply to a request for comment sent via the Russian Press Service.
The Lithuanian investigative files offered an unusually detailed picture of how the system worked. One of the alleged organizers was Andrei Baburov, the former submarine commander and godfather of Kovacs’ son. He allegedly coordinated the transport of the modified massage devices from Russia, drawing on old contacts, including former naval comrades and acquaintances in the Baltic states. Baburov did not reply to a request for comment.
Such personal connections are typical, according to the VSD. Recruits are often linked through “family or social ties,” the Lithuanian report says. Many have financial problems, no jobs or criminal records. They are recruited for individual assignments and do not necessarily know what lies behind them. The less they know, the less they can reveal if they are arrested. And anyone who gets caught can be replaced. “Their main motivation is the desire to make money quickly,” the report states.
Two years after the parcel attacks, operations of this kind had become a growing concern for European security agencies. In August 2026, two explosive-laden drones detonated at Leipzig/Halle Airport, while a third crashed into a Ukrainian cargo aircraft. Among the suspects was a longtime acquaintance of Smolyaninov.
Shortly afterward, two Bulgarians allegedly threw incendiary devices near defense companies in Munich. Investigators suspected the GRU was behind the incident. In Romania, a fire broke out next to an arms factory. Starlink installations were set ablaze in Poland and Bulgaria, leading to further arrests. The GRU has seemingly turned the disposable-agent model into a mass-production operation.
Disposable
On the phone, Vasilij Kovacs sounds agitated. Speaking rapidly in Russian, he tries to explain himself, only to circle back over the same ground. “It was a crime committed so that it would be solved,” he says.
In Kovacs’ trial, the witnesses for the prosecution have already testified and the defense is preparing to call its own. With hearings scheduled well into January, a verdict is a long way off. Kovacs sees himself as the victim of a conspiracy. He believes the Russians deliberately drew him into the affair to make him, a Ukrainian citizen, a convenient villain. European investigators, he argues, only identified the most obvious participants without pursuing the people truly behind the operation.
He says it was Baburov who lured him into the trap, but he does not believe his former friend worked for the Kremlin. “They threw him away, too,” Kovacs said. Baburov, he says, was an opponent of the Russian government.
Kovacs is reluctant to answer questions about himself. Asked about his background, he says he was born in western Ukraine and had worked as a businessman. Had he worked at sea? “I’m just an amateur.” Then he interrupted: “But let’s move away from talking about me.”
He prefers to discuss what he sees as inconsistencies in the investigation. The weight of the massage pillows he transported does not match the weight of the parcels eventually shipped, he says. In his cell, he has filled a sheet of paper with tightly packed notes. Why are key figures behind the operation standing trial in Warsaw rather than Vilnius? What information was being withheld from the Lithuanian court? If the cargo had passed through Moldova, why was it not inspected at the border?
Other questions he’s less eager to address. What about the pistol with its serial number filed off, or the cellphone jammer found at his home? He was only renting the property, he says. They did not belong to him.
A photograph from the opening of his trial shows Kovacs sitting in the dock, unshaven, wearing a baseball cap beneath a hood. He looks tired. In another photograph, taken before his arrest, he sits on a motocross bike with his grandson perched in front of him, showing the boy how to hold the handlebars. He’s wearing the same cap, but with the bill turned backward. He looks carefree, almost boyish.
Viola Lisija, Kovacs’ 37-year-old daughter, knows the man in that photograph better than almost anyone. “He may be the person I’m closest to in my life,” she says. On the day he was arrested, she was supposed to meet him. She was at a playground in Riga with her son, now 7, when she learned what had happened. “My son loves his grandpa very much,” she says.
Her father had arrived in Latvia as the Soviet Union was collapsing. He initially worked in forestry before going into business, buying and selling forest land and acquiring stakes in Russian companies, including a shoe factory and an ice cream manufacturer. “Those were probably his best years,” Lisija said.
Around 2014, Russian authorities accused Kovacs of being a Ukrainian spy, according to his daughter. He was forced to stop traveling to Russia and give up his business interests there. Back in Latvia, he occasionally earned money sailing yachts from one port to another for their owners.
His background may help explain why Kovacs was of interest to the people behind the parcel operation. He had contacts in Russia, traveled between the Baltic countries and occasionally took on assignments. His daughter believed his previous troubles with the Russian authorities might also have made him a target.
Yet parts of her father’s life remained a mystery even to her. Had he ever moved in shady circles? “I really don’t know,” Lisija says. After the collapse of the Soviet Union, she noted, entrepreneurship and organized crime were often intertwined. Her father came from a different era. She says she never saw her father with a gun. “There were never any stories that made me think: Aha, he’s disappearing at night or doing something strange.”
Kovacs is struggling in prison. He has high blood pressure and complains of headaches. His family, too, is close to breaking point. Lisija’s son misses his grandfather. Every other day, the boy asks about him. She tells him Grandpa is at sea.
“I tell him he’s enjoying life to the fullest,” Lisija says. “I say, ‘He loves the sea, he’s a captain, and he’s off on long voyages around the world.’”
For now, at least, the boy believes her.
Lennart Pfahler is an investigative reporter at WELT. Artur Weigandt is a freelance journalist based in Prague.

Beneath the chandeliers and oil paintings of his Presidential Palace, Finland’s president Alexander Stubb sat down next to his old friend Jonas Gahr Støre, the Norwegian prime minister, to call Vladimir Putin.
They hoped such a dramatic and direct intervention with Russia’s leader would demonstrate European resolve.
Instead, the conversation on a damp autumn morning in Helsinki triggered the biggest rift among Nordic allies since Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine — and exposed Europe’s wider divisions over how to deal with Moscow at a pivotal moment in the push for peace.
As Russian and Ukrainian negotiators prepare for talks with Donald Trump’s envoys in Abu Dhabi this week, the fallout from the call is still reverberating across Europe. Governments are arguing over who should represent Europe in future negotiations and remain divided over a question at the heart of the debate: Does engaging Putin help deliver peace, or simply reward aggression?
Underlying European anxiety is another dilemma: Can America be trusted to broker a fair deal for them and most of all for Ukraine?
EU leaders will grapple with these questions at an informal summit in Dublin this week. Few involved expect them to agree.
In an interview with POLITICO in Oslo, Støre explained why he and Stubb decided to call a leader waging hybrid warfare on Europe and killing Ukrainian civilians with daily drone and missile strikes.
“We work closely with our European partners in supporting Ukraine, but the only voice reaching Moscow comes from Washington,” Støre said. “And you know, we have good and open relations with the American negotiators, with the American administration, but this [war] happens in Europe. And living month by month, thinking that this war will end by Europe not talking to Moscow, I think, is an illusion.”
Other countries sharing a border — and a history — with Putin’s Russia profoundly disagree.
“Europe should not be in a mediator’s position,” Estonia’s Prime Minister Kristen Michal told POLITICO in another interview. “You should not take the role of trying to please the dictator.”
Based on interviews with politicians, diplomats and officials, many granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters, this is the inside story of a phone call that shook Europe.
The Trump shock
Europe has struggled for influence over the stop-start Ukraine peace process ever since Trump returned to the White House in early 2025, promptly picked up the phone to Putin and ended U.S. financial assistance to Kyiv.
Trump’s interventions shattered the transatlantic consensus built under his predecessor Joe Biden, offering Putin the prospect of an advantageous ceasefire and a return to the international fold.
The U.S.-Iran war this year interrupted momentum but Trump returned to the topic of Ukraine again in October, criticizing President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for continuing to attack Russian energy infrastructure, while declaring that Putin’s side had been “fine”.
Fearing the negotiations were drifting toward collapse, Stubb and Støre intervened. Støre hosted Zelenskyy and Trump envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo in an attempt to repair relations. Stubb, who also attended, declared the meeting on Oct. 20 had put the peace process “back on track.”
But 24 hours later, Witkoff again stunned European leaders by meeting Putin in St. Petersburg and praising him as a “humanitarian.”
After consulting Zelenskyy, the two Nordic leaders concluded they could not leave Trump, Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner as the only Western figures speaking directly to Putin.
Old friends
Stubb and Støre have known each other for years and worked closely on Russian affairs when they both served as foreign ministers. They talk and text frequently — and like to pair up on key files despite coming from different political backgrounds.
They had quietly explored the idea of a joint call to the Kremlin for months and concluded that reviving momentum would be critical ahead of renewed negotiations in Abu Dhabi.
Europeans, many officials privately acknowledge, no longer trusted Washington to defend either Europe’s interests or Ukraine’s.
“We have to ask the question in Europe if we feel that someone else should have the contact and the discussion on our behalf,” one EU government official said. “Is the feeling that the U.S. should own our objectives?”
“It’s important that Donald Trump is not the only leader from the West who talks to Putin,” another senior European official said. “We need pro-Ukraine leaders putting their messages to Putin too.”
So, almost five years after Russia’s diplomatic isolation began, Stubb and Støre decided to call the Kremlin. The Nordic team reached out to Putin’s officials and agreed parameters for the conversation. Each side would take turns to deliver their prepared messages, without interruption from the other.
Omens in oils
Some of the omens were inauspicious from the start.
As the leaders sat next to each other at the long cabinet table in Stubb’s plush presidential salon on Oct. 27, two large, gilt-framed oil paintings loomed over them, depicting battle scenes from the Crimean War. One canvas shows an Anglo-French naval force retreating under fire on Finnish territory, a reminder of an era two centuries ago when Finland itself was part of the Russian Empire.
According to some accounts, Putin shared his own keen interest in Russia’s past with the two Nordic leaders — delivering a lengthy lesson on Slavic history and the origins of the war in Ukraine.
One senior official familiar with the matter said Stubb and Støre listened patiently during the 90-minute conversation. Other European officials briefed on the call denied that Putin had given the two leaders a history lecture at all, and suggested this claim was Russian spin aimed at humiliating the Europeans.
Støre himself said: “I was present. He didn’t.” Putin has well-worn arguments about the origins of the war, he added. “But in all fairness, he can give his explanation, and we respond to that.”
For their part, the Nordic pair first gave Putin Zelenskyy’s messages — that territorial boundaries can only be discussed at leader level, face to face, and first there must be de-escalation measures. Stubb and his friend then turned to the matter of Baltic Sea security and the need to keep the waterway open for trade.
One reason for holding the call was to try to judge Putin’s state of mind, according to officials. The Norwegian leader said Putin was “rational” and “professional” on the phone. “His arguments were perfectly clearly transmitted.”
Putin took the idea of talks in Abu Dhabi seriously and told the Nordic pair he would instruct his negotiators to prepare for the meeting to explore if progress is possible. “The fact that he picks up that phone, that we have, you know, other ways of reaching, I think that signals, at least that there’s a readiness to sit down.”
But afterwards, Støre was still not convinced that Putin was genuinely open to a deal. Despite their efforts, the Norwegian and Finnish team do not expect a major breakthrough in Abu Dhabi.
Baltic backlash
When Stubb’s office announced the surprise call had happened, the diplomatic blowback played out live in public.
By coincidence, the leaders of Denmark and Sweden, among others, were already gathered in Helsinki for a Nordic Council meeting. Confronted by TV crews, they made little effort to hide their irritation.
“I’m very skeptical about this Norwegian and Finnish initiative,” Denmark’s Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen told broadcasters. “I think we should keep Europe united rather than going it alone.”
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said peace must come through “strength” rather than “appeasement”. Lithuania also criticized the move.
In private, some diplomats were even harsher. “There are too many middle-aged men who want to end up in the history books having solved this war,” one EU diplomat said. “Putin is just gaining from opening up a more normalized dialogue with the rest of the world — and continuing to bomb and kill innocent people in Ukraine.”
Their complaints were not simply over the decision to engage with Putin, but that Stubb and Støre had not properly coordinated with allies beforehand.
Officials familiar with the preparations for the call deny this, insisting that Frederiksen and others including the leadership in France, Germany, and the U.S. were told about the call before it happened. It may just have been that Frederiksen expected more advance warning, and a genuine say over the plan. She said her Finnish and Norwegian counterparts had failed to coordinate the call with “the rest of us.”
Moscow endorsement
Støre is defiant. “She is right, because I did not ask — we did not ask for permission,” he told POLITICO. “We consult each other in the Nordic family, but it is not a mechanism which is that, you know, doing this requires a yes from all the Nordics or from 27 Europeans or beyond.”
Privately, some officials think Støre aggravated the wound in the immediate aftermath, when he pointed out that the EU had been divided on Russia since the war began. “It’s true — it’s just not his place to say it,” one official said. “Norway is not in the EU.”
Stubb and Støre say they never sought to speak for anyone other than the countries they lead, which both border Russia. They talked to Zelenskyy at length before the call to agree what to say to Putin and then briefed him again afterwards.
They had hoped their initiative would bolster Zelenskyy. Instead, the backlash became so intense that the Ukrainian leader stepped in to defend them. “They truly help us,” he said.
The two Nordic leaders also won an endorsement from Moscow. “I believe it was the right thing to do,” Putin said. “After all, there are some people in Europe who do not want to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia … but seek to establish some kind of constructive dialogue.”
Putin’s comments are unlikely to soothe lingering resentments between Nordic neighbors. As one official put it, there may be some lasting “family trauma” for those regional leaders who were not included in the Putin call plan.
For all the northern angst, the episode also exposed a harder truth for Ukraine and its supporters. Despite Trump’s midterm election defeats, he is still dictating the pace of talks. Europe, meanwhile, has no one to match America’s booming voice when it matters in the room.
Clea Caulcutt, Hans von der Burchard, Veronika Melkozerova and Laurens Cerulus contributed reporting.

AND THE COMPOSITION OF PUBLIC INVESTMENT:
EVIDENCE FROM THE DEMOCRATIZATION OF VILLAGES IN INDIA

Mark R. Rosenzweig
