Governance Regimes, Economic Mobility, and the Composition of Public Investment: Evidence 
from the Democratization of Villages in India
Andrew D. Foster and Mark R. Rosenzweig
NBER Working Paper No. 35972
October 2026
JEL No. H11, O12, O13
ABSTRACT
We develop a quantifiable general-equilibrium model of village governance, motivated by India’s 
democratization, to study how political institutions shape public goods provision and economic 
development. The model features two groups, landowners and landless workers, with different 
preferences over public goods such as irrigation, schools, and employment programs. Households 
from both groups can enter nonfarm entrepreneurship, but face credit-dependent entry costs. We 
compare oligarchy, where landowners control public goods decisions, with democracy, where 
electoral competition determines policy based on the relative sizes of the two groups. The calibrated 
model predicts that democratization’s effects on public goods and growth are not uniform; they 
depend on population composition and the ease of occupational mobility through access to credit. 
Using a 37-year village-level panel from India (1971–2006) and exploiting variation in 
democratization driven by state and national reforms, we find strong support for these predictions. 
Financial intermediation shifts landless households’ preferences from wage-enhancing policies 
toward schooling, increasing nonfarm business entry. As a result, democracy provides fewer 
schools than oligarchy when credit is unavailable, but more schools when credit is accessible. We 
also show that transfers to the landless increase schooling under democracy but reduce it under 
oligarchy. These findings highlight how governance structures and economic conditions jointly 
determine the effectiveness of development policies.
Andrew D. Foster
Brown University
Economics Department
and NBER
afoster@brown.edu
Mark R. Rosenzweig
Yale University
Department of Economics
and NBER
mark.rosenzweig@yale.edu
An online appendix is available at http://www.nber.org/data-appendix/w35972
1 
 
1. Introduction 
 Goods allocated by governments (“public goods”) can potentially play a significant role 
in accelerating economic development. For example, infrastructure variables such as roads, 
power grids, irrigation, communication as well as schools are recognized to directly affect real 
income growth. The level, composition, and allocation of public goods depend, however, on a 
number of features of economies including differences in group resources, economic interests, 
and beliefs in economic mobility. Equally important is the identity of those making public goods 
decisions, the form of governance – whether rule is by the wealthiest, by owners of capital, by 
landowners, or by all members of the community. The understanding of how the form of 
governance affects the economy and how political outcomes are shaped by community 
characteristics therefore requires an understanding of the differing interests as well as the 
influence of different groups that reside in a community on public-goods decisions. In addition, 
both inequality between interest groups and the opportunity for economic mobility matter as 
well, with the latter possibly converging group interests. 
 An important feature of governance, qualitatively different from the kinds of spillovers 
from targeted to untargeted groups that operate purely through the market, is that choices are 
made to advance collective interests. While most individuals must operate as price takers, 
interest groups politics can operative collectively to actively manipulate prices through the 
process of public resource allocation. Thus, for example, it is not just that an increase in transfers 
to one group will leads to increased economic activity by the producers who sell to that group, 
but it also means that the first group, if given appropriate influence, may target public resources 
that otherwise increases demand or curtails supply and will thus effect the equilibrium prices that 
will emerge. One therefore cannot just focus on the political interests of different groups but one 
must also consider on how political interests interact with the macroeconomy. 
 In this paper, we assess how democratization - the shift to a form of government in which 
all community members have a vote from one in which only a subset effectively control public 
resource allocations - affects the composition of public goods and how therefore policy 
interventions affect the economy via a change in the composition of public goods. Focusing on 
democratization in a rural economy, we construct a quantifiable, general-equilibrium model with 
an agricultural sector selling a tradeable good and a nonfarm non-tradeable sector that has entry 
2 
 
costs. The economy has two major interest groups – landowners, who produce a tradable good, 
and the landless - that reap differential benefits from specific public goods but with opportunities 
to shift to nonfarm entrepreneurship. In our setting we treat the initial distribution of 
landownership, and thus inequality, as fixed, but vary the degree to which there is economic 
mobility via changes in the cost of entry into the nonfarm, non-tradeable sector. 
In this setting, we compare public goods outcomes under two governance regimes, one in 
which the landed are the sole public-goods decision-makers (oligarchy) to one in which all 
members of the landed and the landless classes vote in contested elections that determine which 
political platforms defining public goods composition wins out. The principal implication is that 
the relative size of the two interest groups and occupational mobility costs affect how each 
governance regime affects the composition of public goods. In particular, the model illuminates 
how the relative population shares affect directly the magnitude and distribution of the returns to 
specific public goods and how the relative influence of the two groups differs under the two 
political regimes, mediated by the costs of business entry and thus economic upgrading, leading 
to very different public goods portfolios from the same regime and across regimes. 
 The general-equilibrium model is quantified using household survey data and a new 
annual panel data set of Indian villages describing the evolution of key local public goods and 
the change to democratic governance at the village level over a 37-year period, 1971-2006, 
spurred by state and federal constitutional amendments, to both provide empirically-grounded 
parameter values for the model and to test its implications. A key feature of the model is the 
inclusion of fixed costs of entry into the nonfarm non-tradeable sector that require capital, with 
the cost of acquiring capital (credit costs) depending on the presence of banks. Bank presence 
thus plays an important role in facilitating economic mobility, specifically transforming landless 
wage workers, given sufficient ability, to entrepreneurs whose economic interest then align more 
closely with those of the landed. The survey data indeed show that banks are the principal source 
of loans for initiating a nonfarm enterprise, that bank loans charge significantly lower interest 
rates for such loans compared with informal sources, and that these rural bank loans are as large 
in total as those for agricultural investment. 
The model also highlights the importance of schooling for both farm and nonfarm 
enterprise profitability, relative to its returns in wage work, with household survey data 
providing estimates of these returns in all three occupations. An implication of the model, borne 
3 
 
out by the village panel data, is that the introduction of financial intermediation tends to shift 
landless households from a primary interest in wage augmenting policies towards an interest in 
public schooling investment, which increases entry into the nonfarm sector. These effects are 
more modest among landed households, who already receive a return to schooling through the 
farm sector, leading to a reversal in which while fewer schools are provided under democracy 
relative to oligarchy in the absence of credit, but more schools are provided under democracy 
when credit is accessible. Our findings thus suggest that democratization’s effects on economic 
growth may be negative or positive depending on the composition and interest disparities of 
economic classes as well as on the degree of economic mobility of the poor. 
We also use our calibrated model to carry out a counter-factual analysis of a large cash 
transfer to the poor (landless) households. This is caried out both to show the effects of changes 
in inequality on the public goods allocation but also to demonstrate that the consequences depend 
importantly on the political regimes as well as the availability of credit and thus barriers to 
sectoral mobility. Our simulation mimics that in Eggers et al. (2002) in that the transfer is large 
and externally funded, so it combines a distributional and a macroeconomic income effect. As in 
their article we find general-equilibrium effects on wages and the price of the non-traded good. 
But unlike in their work we examine the effects on local public goods and show that the political 
regime matters and credit availability matter. A striking result is that the exogenous increases in 
transfers to the poor lead to increases in the construction of local public schools under 
democracy but to decreases under oligarchy. 
Another important general implication of our model is that the choice of democracy itself 
depends on the polarity and distribution of interest groups. For example, the group in power may 
resist democratization more intensively the greater it expects there to be a shift in public goods 
priorities, which under democracy will depend on the shares of the interest groups in the 
population. In the Indian case, although village democratization was mandated by constitutional 
amendments, we find that the timing of the shift to village democratic governance from 
oligarchic leadership depended on the share of landless in the village, with the shift delayed the 
larger the landless fraction. In estimating the effect of democratization of public goods 
allocations, we take into account its endogeneity, exploiting the staggered passage of state-level 
constitutional amendments over the 37-year period as instruments. 
4 
 
 Our work contributes to a number of major literatures. One focuses on how perceptions 
of economic mobility shape preferences for redistribution (Alesina and La Ferrara, 2005; 
Kuziemko et al., 2015; Cojocaru, 2014). We show that variation in opportunities for investment 
shape both redistributive preferences but also how they are manifested in actual public goods 
choices via differing political processes. Another literature examines the link between perceived 
mobility and overall public goods levels or one specific public, with or without redistributive 
motives. For example, Dorsch (2010) develops a model that holds income inequality fixed and 
shows that when high-income households prefer less public goods, economic mobility lessens 
even more public goods expenditures. Di Gioacchino et al. (2022) focus on spending on public 
schools, with mobility defined by the persistence of educational attainment across generations. 
Cojocaru et al. (2025) show empirically that differing perceptions of economic mobility across 
countries affect willingness to pay taxes financing public schools, but do not examine why 
perceptions vary across countries or their effects on other public goods. Wiese and Eriksen 
(2024) examine how mobility prospects matter for the demand for public school and health 
expenditures but treat them as satisfying the same need. 
Our framework differs from and extends the work on perceptions of mobility and public 
goods in two ways. First, we examine the portfolio of public goods rather than focusing on one 
public good or total public goods. Second, we focus on the public goods outcomes emanating 
from two political regimes, for a given public resource constraint, with the mixture of public 
goods reflecting the differing interest of the community groups, the degree of mobility between 
them, and who makes public decisions. Third, we vary opportunities for economic advancement 
in the economy. That is, we model the root causes of perceptions of mobility or the returns to 
effort (Benabou and Tirole, 2006), showing why and how they may vary across economies 
depending on the availability of credit, a feature that is treated as exogenous in the literature 
examining empirically the links between mobility perceptions and public goods. 
There is also a vast literature in economics and political science focused on the question 
of whether democracy positively or negatively affects economic growth. It is fair to say that the 
results are mixed. For example, Acemoglu et al. (2019) using a panel of 170 countries from 
1960-2010 find that democratization increases economic growth. However, when the 
observations are restricted to the time series covering the years 2001-2019 for the same countries 
and using the same methodology, democracy appears to reduce economic growth (Narita and 
5 
 
Sudo, 2021). A common characteristic of this cross-country literature directly estimating the 
causal effects of democratization on growth, whatever the data used, or the identification strategy 
employed, is the assumption that the effect of democracy is the same across all countries and the 
absence of attention to mechanisms. Our analysis shows that this homogeneity assumption is 
likely incorrect and quantifies the key parameters describing the economy that shape political 
outcomes by political regime. It also provides insights into the mechanisms by which the form of 
governance affects economic development via shifting the composition of public goods in 
response to the interests of economic classes in the economy depending on who has more control 
over public resources and on what opportunities are in place for economic mobility. 
 Bardhan and Mookerhjee (2010) also focus on how public programs are affected by the 
interests of landowners under democracy in Indian villages. Employing a similar model of 
democracy that we embed in our general-equilibrium model of the economy, they show that the 
share of landowners in the village importantly affected polices on land reform and that party 
allegiances were substantially less important than economic interests. They did not, however, 
extend the analysis to the portfolio of public goods, nor compare policy outcomes prior to 
democratization. 
 A number of studies have examined the role of governance in the spatial allocation of 
public goods. The closest study to ours that looks directly at democratization and its relationship 
to public goods is by Burgess et al. (2015). They examined how the shift in governance regime 
from autocracy to democracy in Kenya led to a more efficient spatial allocation of roads. In 
particular, they showed that new road construction was more concentrated in locations 
dominated by the ruler’s own ethnic group under autocracy than under democracy. A limitation 
of this study is that there is no attention to the level of road expenditures relative to other public 
goods spending under the two regimes nor clarity as to why the regimes shifted.2

definition of democracy is somewhat amorphous. In cross-country studies, “democracy” is typically an

 Studies using Indian data on democratized villages have also showed that leader 
characteristics matter even under democracy for the spatial allocation of public goods. Besley et 
al. (2011) find that presidents of local councils with representatives from multiple villages

 Finally, Martinez-Bravo et al. (2020) exploit panel data on democratized villages in 
China to examine how elections affect public goods outcomes. Unlike in India, the move to 
village democracy in China was from top-down governance by a central authority.3 In their

conflict, and they show evidence, consistent with their organizational view of local political

 a. Measuring village democratization. As noted, India initiated in the last two decades of 
the Twentieth Century at both the national and state levels reforms aimed at transforming village 
governing authorities into democratic organizations. In recognition of the importance of these 
activities, we incorporated a set of questions on village governance in the 1999-2000 and 2006-8 
re-surveys of rural households administered by the National Council of Economic Research 
(NCAER). This survey was a continuation of the Rural Economic Development Survey (REDS) 
that was last undertaken in the 1981-82 crop year and initiated in 1968 with a complete survey in 
1971. The survey, providing individual-, household-, and village-level information for a sample 
of villages and households in 16 of the major states of India consists of a core stratified random 
sample of approximately 5000 households located, initially, in 253 villages based on a sample 
frame designed in 1968, the first round of the panel. 
 A key feature of the data is that the 1999-2000 and 2006-8 rounds included a village-
level questionnaire that elicited the history of changes by year in the village governance 
structure, defined as the individual or group that “makes decisions about common resources.” 
There were six governance classifications information on which was provided by a set of 
knowledgeable village informants. - ‘traditional panchayat’, ‘elected panchayat’, ‘village 
headman’, ‘wealthy individual’, ‘regional government official’, and ‘none’- plus a miscellaneous 
category. We will consider a village as ‘democratic’ each year if it falls in the category of 
‘elected panchayat’ and elections took place. The 2006-8 round also included information on 
elections for the current and last two elected panchayats. From this information we constructed 
an annual village-level time-series of village democratization covering the 36-year period from 
1971 to 2006 for the 242 sample villages represented in all four survey rounds. 
 The shifts in village governance to democracy were not random events but were in large 
part responses to state-level amendments. To identify the shifts in the effects of variation in the 
landless share by governance regime we use the state level timing in these governance 
amendments as instruments, as described below. These sets of state-level amendments can be 
roughly classified in three stages, the first being efforts in Rajasthan and Andhra Pradesh in the 
late 1950's and early 1960's to democratize local community development organizations, 
following the recommendations of the Balawantray Mehta Committee of 1957. The second-stage 
is demarked by the Asoka Mehta Committee of 1977, which was followed by legislation in four 
states - West Bengal, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Jammu and Kashmir - encouraging the

9. Counterfactuals: the effects of cash transfers to the poor 
39 
 
Having established that the quantitative model captures the basic features of the data we 
explore the effects of an externally-funded large cash transfer to the landless poor on the 
composition of public goods under the two regimes of oligarchy and democracy. We do this for a 
fixed landless concentration, which we set at the relatively high value of 0.6, which will make 
more stark the differences between the two political regimes, although the results are similar 
qualitatively for landless shares closer to the mean of 0.35 
Figures 7-9 display the effects of the cash dump on three public goods outcomes. As 
expected, employment programs are zeroed out under oligarchy. (Figure 7). There is also a 
substantial decline in employment programs as transfers to the landless increase. This result may 
be attributed to the fact that these transfers are provided as a traded good thus increasing the 
interest among the landless in lowering the price of the non-traded good; this makes raising the 
wage through public employment less attractive to the landless. This effect is also evident when 
banks are present where the still larger return to non-farm goods further diminishes interest in 
increasing the wage among the landless. 
The effects of transfers on school investment and irrigation investments (Figures 8 and 9) 
are in accord with the model. At low levels of transfers with high credit costs, school 
construction is higher when oligarchs are in charge, reflecting the returns to schooling in 
agriculture and the absence of schooling returns for wage workers. However, the oligarchs 
choose to decrease expenditures on public schools with increased transfers to the landless. Under 
democracy we see the opposite effect – public school expenditures increase from the lower level 
as the transfer amounts increase such that at higher levels of transfers school expenditures are 
actually higher under democracy than under oligarchy. As we have shown, the key factor for the 
rise in public school expenditures is the increased interest in depressing the nontraded goods 
price among the landless. Under democracy there is a relatively strong interest in expanding 
schools in order to allow the nonfarm sector to grow. The effect is even more dramatic when 
banks are present and the nonfarm sector becomes more active – again with credit less costly, 
public-school construction is higher than under oligarchy and the difference increases as the 
landless receive larger cash transfers. 
Why under oligarchy do public schooling expenditures fall as the landless receive higher 
transfers? This result emerges because of the difference in the value of public schools between 
the landed and the landless. Because the schooling of the wealthy landed is high and they can 
40 
 
afford private schools they benefit less from increased public-school access, as is evident in the 
data, and they can increase their role in the supply of nonfarm goods by reducing the availability 
of public schools, which benefit the landless, and thus make nonfarm activity less viable for 
them. The mirror image of this crossover, arising from the fixed budget constraint, is evident in 
Figure 9 in the irrigation subsidy. Overall, expenditures on irrigation are lower in the presence of 
banks and oligarchy and democracy cross when banks are not present. 
10. Conclusion 
It has long been recognized that the process of economic development can flounder if 
inadequate attention is given to the responses of individual households and markets to incentives. 
But there has been less attention to the fact that public investment generally plays an increasingly 
important role in the process of economic development and that choices over how public 
resources are allocated are likely to be importantly affected by the extant political institutions. It 
may thus be difficult to understand the impact of a policy or other source of economic change 
without understanding how the interests of particular interest groups are affected as well as how 
those interests are adjudicated through the political system. 
In this paper, we constructed a model that incorporates the mechanisms by which 
inequality between groups in both economic interests and endowments, economic mobility, and 
endogenous structural change alter the set of public goods affecting economic development 
depending on the political regime. The model, quantified and tested using both rural panel survey 
data and annual time-series of village level data from India over the period 1971-2006 when 
Indian villages democratized, captures key features of low-income countries. In particular, it 
highlights the fact that landownership is a key determinant of wealth, and in the absence of 
opportunities for entrepreneurship in the nonfarm sector interests are sharply divided between the 
landed and the landless. Under these circumstances the weighting of the political system towards 
landed or landless households will alter public investment decisions, and sensitivity of public 
goods outcomes to political regime will be larger the more unequal are landholdings. We show 
that circumstances change markedly when access to capital gives both landed and landless 
households the ability to raise the capital necessary to start a nonfarm business. This emergence 
will tend to create interest groups within each category of landholding along the dimension of 
entrepreneurial ability and to reduce average differences across groups. Most noticeably, we 
find, in accord with our general-equilibrium model incorporating a farm and nonfarm, non-
41 
 
tradeable sector, while democratization leads to greater public work programs and less 
investment in school construction when banks are not present, the emergence of banks, providing 
lower-cost loans for business investment compared with informal sources, leads to less 
investment in work programs and moderates the negative effect of democracy on schools. 
Our results indicate that democratization has heterogeneous effects on public goods 
choices that affect economic development depending on the degree of inequality, the polarization 
of economic interests, and economic opportunity, with financial intermediation playing a key 
role. There is thus no one answer to whether democracy enhances growth; it depends. We also 
used the quantitative model to examine the effects of an external cash transfer intervention on 
public-goods choice. We found that depending both on the form of governance and the 
availability of financial intermediation, this intervention has dramatically different effects. For 
example, our simulations indicate that an expansion in externally-financed cash transfers to the 
poor can lead to either lower or higher schooling construction depending on the political regime 
and the degree to which there are lower costs of economic mobility in the form of increased 
entrepreneurial activity in the non-farm non-tradeable sector. This suggests that one must be 
cautious as well about the external validity of any scaled-up intervention documented in a single 
place.

ABSTRACT
We develop a property-rights based approach for defining welfare weights in economic models of 
climate change. Whether there is a "right to pollute" or a "right to no pollution" is increasingly 
contested in legislatures, courts, and international climate negotiations. We show how these notions 
of property rights can provide the basis for "Coasean welfare weights" that are applicable in 
multilateral public goods settings. Distributional questions are addressed through positive analysis, 
conditional on property rights, rather than normative views about redistribution. The implied 
transfers are consistent with a bargained solution over the net benefits of addressing climate change 
and reflect the value of property rights over emissions. The approach defines efficient allocations 
that generate Pareto improvements, in contrast to commonly used Negishi weights. We implement 
the approach in a global integrated assessment model to quantify what countries have at stake in 
ongoing political and legal debates about emissions-related property rights.

1 Introduction
A large and growing body of evidence shows that climate change will cause substantial and
highly uneven damages across countries (e.g., Diaz, 2016; Carleton et al., 2022; Hultgren et
al., 2025). Less attention has been given to the way that resolving climate change through
collective action will also have distributional consequences. These consequences arise not
only because of heterogeneity in avoided damages across countries, but also because of dif-
ferences in abatement costs and the extent to which international transfers may (or may not)
occur. Resolving climate change among countries is at its core a global public goods prob-
lem (Barrett, 2007; Buchholz and Sandler, 2021), and a seminal insight of Samuelson (1954)
is that public goods problems do not, in general, have a unique Pareto efficient solution.
Instead, there is a set of efficient allocations that differ in their distributional consequences.
Solving public goods problems, such as climate change, therefore requires selecting among
allocations on the basis of some criterion beyond efficiency, and how economists make this
choice remains an enduring source of debate.
The choice is typically framed as the need for analysts to choose welfare weights across
countries or regions for use in a global planner’s social welfare function (Dietz, 2024). A
common approach is to use a variant of Negishi weights, where the resulting Pareto efficient
allocation is the one that arises without international transfers (Nordhaus and Yang, 1996;
Manne and Richels, 2005; Leimbach et al., 2010; Krusell and Smith Jr., 2022; Traeger, 2023;
Alsina-Pujols, 2026). The approach is often understood as allowing analysts to separate the
problem of climate change from global income inequality, addressing the inefficiency of cli-
mate change while sidestepping normative judgments about distributional justice (Nordhaus
and Yang, 1996; Hassler and Krusell, 2012; Barrage, 2020). This interpretation is nev-
ertheless criticized for failing to recognize implicit normative assumptions (Stanton, 2011;
Kelleher, 2018). The main alternative in the literature is more explicitly normative, whereby
analysts use social welfare functions with some degree of inequality aversion (Chichilnisky
and Heal, 1994; Tol, 1997, 2002; Dennig et al., 2015; Budolfson et al., 2021; Lang, 2026).
These social welfare functions introduce a redistributive motive, but critics of the approach
argue that the implied transfers may require more international redistribution than countries
are willing to undertake. 1

A Coasean solution is then obtained through Nash (1950) bargaining, which defines a

A key result is that Coasean welfare weights always result in a Pareto improvement
relative to the corresponding reference allocation, that is, all countries are made (weakly)
better off. This feature of the planner’s solution is important because the distributional
consequences of resolving climate change are central to the design and political feasibility
of international policy. In contrast, Pareto improvements do not necessarily arise with the
use of Negishi weights, highlighting their distributional consequences despite their frequent
interpretation as being distributionally neutral. We also use our model to identify conditions
under which a specific country will make or receive a transfer with Coasean welfare weights,
along with the conditions that dictate whether a country prefers one property-rights regime
over another.

Finally, by comparing reference allocations for one property-rights regime with the efficient

rights rather than address climate change. In particular, we illustrate how some countries
prefer the inefficient allocation under one set of property rights to the efficient allocation
under the alternative set.
The overarching contribution of this paper is to show how the choice of welfare weights in
climate economics can be grounded in a positive analysis of property rights. The approach
differs fundamentally from the use of inequality-averse social welfare functions and associated
equity weights, which impose a normative criterion of distributive equity. While we do not
prescribe how property rights should be assigned, we note that the choice itself is actively
debated and has normative content (Fleurbaey, 2008). Nevertheless, separating considera-
tion of the distributional consequences of property rights from questions about efficiency is
familiar territory for analysts of environmental and natural resource problems (Coase, 1960;
Libecap, 1990; Deryugina et al., 2021).
The approach is also distinct from the standard use of Negishi weights in climate models,
though we argue it is more closely aligned with Negishi’s original formulation with respect to
the role of initial endowments. Negishi’s (1960) original analysis applies to a private-goods
economy with no market failures, showing a correspondence between the decentralized equi-
librium and the appropriately weighted planner’s problem. When applied in climate models,
however, the public goods market failure is central, and Negishi weights are typically used
to implement an efficient allocation with an assumed no-transfer rule (e.g., Nordhaus and

6 Conclusion
This paper develops a property-rights based approach for defining welfare weights in cli-
mate economics. We show how familiar notions of the “right to pollute” or the “right to
no pollution” can provide the basis for Coasean welfare weights. The approach anchors
questions about distributional outcomes among countries in a positive analysis, conditional
on property rights, rather than on normative principles of distributional justice. Transfers
that arise among countries are not driven by a redistributive motive that a global planner
imposes. Instead, they follow the logic of Coasean bargaining, adapted to a multilateral
public goods setting, in accordance with the principles of either the “beneficiary pays” for
emissions reductions, or the “polluter pays” for emissions increases. In contrast to standard
approaches for choosing welfare weights in the literature, our approach obtains a globally
efficient allocation that is always a Pareto improvement for all countries, making the solution
potentially appealing among sovereign countries.
The framework is novel in the way it connects the insights of several seminal contributions.
Samuelson (1954) identifies the initial problem with the inherent need for welfare weights
when choosing among Pareto efficient allocations involving provision of a public good. Coase
(1960) shows how establishing property rights can resolve externality problems, and we
show how the same logic can apply to the global public goods problem of climate change,
with property rights over the right to pollute or not. We then show how Nash (1950)
bargaining identifies a particular Coasean solution, and calibrating Negishi (1960) weights
to the resulting Pareto efficient level of consumption in each country defines a corresponding
global social welfare function for potential use in IAMs.
The fundamental difference between Coasean welfare weights and Negishi weights as
commonly used in climate economics (e.g., Nordhaus and Yang, 1996) is the level of con-
sumption to which the weights are calibrated. Both approaches respect the initial distri-
bution of private-good endowments. The standard Negishi approach imposes a constraint
of no transfers among countries, yet as we make clear, distributional consequences arise
because countries differ in the net benefits of changes in emissions. In contrast, Coasean
welfare weights imply transfers among countries, but importantly, they are consistent with
a decentralized, Pareto-improving bargaining procedure. The standard Negishi approach is
often justified as the only way for IAMs to address climate change without simultaneously
addressing global income inequality. Our approach, however, provides an alternative, where
transfers reflect the value of property rights, rather than normative views about inequality.
At the same time, the resulting allocations still depend in part on the initial distribution
of endowments, as with Negishi weights, and to the extent there are equity concerns with
32
initial endowments, there may be equity concerns with the resulting efficient allocations.
We employ a relatively simple IAM and begin to quantify what countries (or regions)
have at stake in ongoing debates about emissions-related property rights. While the total
transfers that arise under either property-rights regime are not large enough to materi-
ally change the distribution of wealth across countries, the magnitudes are large enough to
have meaningful effects for certain countries. Underlying many of the results is the way
that countries with large benefits of emissions relative to climate damages tend to prefer
“right to pollute,” whereas countries with large climate damages relative to the benefits of
emissions tend to prefer “right to no pollution.” Cross-country heterogeneity and the result-
ing distributional consequences of alternative property-rights regimes help to explain why
climate-related property rights are sparking growing debate around the world.
Finally, we acknowledge that our quantitative application is relatively simple in order to
focus on the fundamental ideas, and future research can further clarify the consequences of
Coasean welfare weights compared to other approaches using more detailed IAMs. A natural
next step is to implement the approach in a dynamic IAM, one that captures the intertem-
poral nature of climate change and the potential value of property rights. We also focus
throughout on the Nash bargaining solution to simulate a decentralized Coasean bargain-
ing procedure, but alternative solution concepts might be worth considering in future work
(e.g., other bargaining approaches or definitions of core stability). Additionally, we consider
reference allocations based solely on RP and RnP, but our framework could accommodate
other considerations too, such as historical or differentiated responsibilities among countries.
Future research might also consider more explicit links to climate policy instruments, as
we focus on efficient allocations without regard to policies needed to implement them. For
example, one approach would be to implement globally efficient carbon taxes combined with
international transfers, but another is an emissions trading system with a particular alloca-
tion of permits that reflects the endowments implied here. In these settings, Coasean welfare
weights can be used to characterize specific Pareto-improving policy packages.
33

- April 2025 controls on dysprosium, terbium, and yttrium remain operative, making license approval rates and shipment data stronger stress indicators than diplomatic headlines.

Professionals such as bankers, owners of currency or cryptocurrency exchanges, lawyers and accountants could end up in the dock, even facing prison sentences, if they turn a blind eye in transactions such as those for granting golden visas to foreign clients and fail to notify the authorities when they have even a suspicion that the sums involved, usually large, are the proceeds of money laundering.
This change is being introduced along with a series of other provisions, aiming to create a stronger legal framework to combat money laundering within the first months of 2027.
A separate chapter of the new framework includes a series of measures to quickly identify the real beneficial owners hiding behind corporate structures, often short-lived ones, and to put a stop to the creation of such “legal vehicles” fronted by “straw men” who pose as managers.
“TA NEA Weekend” today reveals the major changes that are about to be legislated, with the aim of tackling the crime of laundering the proceeds of illegal activities more effectively, a problem that is not unique to Greece.
This complex task has been assigned to a working group of about 30 bodies, coordinated by the Anti-Money Laundering Authority, which in recent years has intervened in dozens of criminal cases, mapped suspicious money flows and has the know-how to deal with such criminal offenses.
Safeguards
“A superhuman effort is being made so that the draft law is delivered by the end of 2026 and the required process can move forward immediately,” says Charalambos Vourliotis, president of the Independent Anti-Money Laundering Authority and honorary deputy prosecutor of the Supreme Court.
“With the new safeguards, the aim is for lawmakers, and indeed at a pan-European level, not to be left chasing after criminals who launder huge sums undisturbed, but to be able to prevent such offenses by using new, modern tools,” said sources familiar with the upcoming changes. The new legal framework will consist of 100 articles, with the goal of transforming the fight against dirty money in Greece from the first months of 2027.
Recent cases, such as those involving the “To Horiatiko” bakery chain, Pizza Fan and the NGO Paidiki Chara, in which the defendants are also being investigated for money laundering, show the scale of a problem that is not only Greek.
7 Changes
According to information obtained by TA NEA, the main proposals and changes from the working group include the following:
- The role of the Anti-Money Laundering Authority will be upgraded, with its participation in decision-making at the EU level.
- The rules for combating money laundering will be unified across the EU, creating a new, broader regulatory framework.
- The legal framework will be tightened for banks, investment firms, insurance companies, currency exchanges, cryptocurrency exchanges, lawyers, accountants and others involved in golden visa cases. How will this work?
According to information, any of these professionals who suspect during a transaction that money laundering may be taking place must immediately notify the relevant authorities. Otherwise, they risk being held criminally liable themselves, facing even prison sentences.
- Stricter safeguards will be introduced for legal entities, along with additional requirements to identify the real beneficial owners of various entities, in order to prevent them from being run by “straw men,” as happened for years in the recently uncovered “To Horiatiko” case.
- Sanctions imposed across Europe will be linked to the anti-money laundering framework.
- Stricter training requirements will be set for staff dealing with money laundering, with particular emphasis on four principles: skills, confidentiality, integrity and discretion.
- The list of people required to submit asset declarations will be gradually expanded between 2027 and 2028 to include figures from professional sports. This will start with professional soccer, followed by other sports such as basketball and volleyball. The provision takes on particular importance following the recent arrests in the case of alleged fixed basketball games.
European Directive
It is worth noting that the legal framework on money laundering is based mainly on European directives. In Greece, the most recent law on combating money laundering has been in force since 2018, when the 2015 European directive was transposed into national law.
Specifically, this is Law 4557/2018 on the “Prevention and suppression of money laundering and terrorist financing and other provisions,” which incorporated Directive 2015/849/EU.
However, that directive has been replaced by a newer one from 2024. As a result, Greece must now transpose the new European directive into national law by the first months of 2027. This is Directive (EU) 2024/1640, a key pillar of the new, unified European framework for preventing and combating money laundering and terrorist financing.

The Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control on November 6 designated eight money services businesses based in Canada that enable the Iranian regime, sanctioned entities associated with the regime, and other illicit actors that move assets into and out of Iran.
As part of Operation Economic Outcast, the action targets companies that facilitate the exchange of Iranian rials and other currencies for digital assets to enable international transactions involving Iran. Many of these businesses have facilitated transactions with sanctioned Iranian digital asset exchanges, as well as with digital asset addresses associated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). The State Department described the designations as action against eight digital asset service providers that help the Iranian regime evade sanctions and fund terrorism.
“Canada cannot be a safe haven for illicit financial facilitators that provide sanctions evasion services to the Iranian regime and its proxies,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent. “Treasury will pursue and disrupt the Iranian regime’s financial channels anywhere in the world.”
The designated entities are Diverse Trade Inc (doing business as Million Exchange), 1380079 BC Limited and Top PC Technician Inc (both doing business as Amin Exchange), NIA Nations Currency Ltd, 2397639 Ontario Ltd (doing business as Farah Exchange), CCC Inc, B Galaxy Inc (doing business as Cryptoyal), and Darvish Exchange. Several of the targets also worked with narco-trafficker and former Olympic snowboarder Ryan Wedding, who was apprehended in January 2026. Wedding used money exchange businesses in the Vancouver and Toronto areas to launder billions of dollars in drug proceeds, converting cash to digital assets for transfer abroad.
This action was coordinated with the Department of the Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) and FINTRAC, Canada’s financial intelligence unit, as well as the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA). It reflects the Trump Administration’s whole-of-government effort to combat the illicit use of digital assets for drug trafficking. The designations follow previous OFAC sanctions on Iranian digital asset exchanges, including the June 2, 2026 designations of Nobitex, Wallex, Bitpin, and Ramzinex, and the August 7, 2026 designations of Aban Tether Exchange and SHPS Shelbit.
The State Department noted that several of the designated businesses also laundered proceeds from drug trafficking, showing how the same illicit networks serve both Iran and criminal organizations. As part of Operation Economic Outcast, launched in August to sever economic lifelines sustaining the Iranian regime and its IRGC, the United States will continue to cut off revenue used for terrorism, weapons proliferation, and proxies. The designations are imposed pursuant to Executive Order 13902, which targets the Iranian digital asset sector among other key sectors of the Iranian economy.
As a result of this action, all property and interests in property of the designated persons that are in the United States or in the possession or control of U.S. persons are blocked. OFAC’s regulations generally prohibit all transactions by U.S. persons or within the United States that involve any property or interests in property of designated persons. Violations of U.S. sanctions may result in civil or criminal penalties.

As global climate negotiators and government officials convene for the annual United Nations climate summit, the scientific organization they rely on to guide their decisions is mired in gridlock and short on funds.
Since 1990, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has produced influential global reports in cycles. Its 2013 and 2014 reports provided the scientific foundation for the 2015 Paris climate agreement, which continues to shape international climate policy. But the IPCC suspended its mid-October meeting without approving a budget for next year or agreeing on a timetable for publishing upcoming reports.
The political disputes that derailed the meeting rattled many of the scientists who devote hundreds of hours, often without pay, to assess the latest climate research across dozens of disciplines, from ice sheets and glaciers to forests and agriculture. Their work not only tracks the science of a changing climate, it also identifies ways to cut greenhouse gas emissions and helps communities adapt to increasingly severe climate impacts.
More than 100 IPCC scientists expressed their concern about the future of the panel in an Oct. 19 open letter, asking political leaders to provide it with adequate resources. The scientists reaffirmed their commitment to the work, but warned that, as climate impacts intensify, governments must ensure the panel can produce timely assessments of climate risks and potential solutions when they are needed. They also called for a process that gives all countries an equitable voice, rather than allowing wealthy, industrialized nations to dominate.
The IPCC will resume its session online in December, after the annual COP, the Conference of Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. This year’s event, COP31, begins next week in Antalya, Turkey. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change continually informs the negotiations with science updates, but political tensions have affected its budget and timelines for upcoming reports.
Governments decide voluntarily each year how much to contribute to the panel’s annual budget of $9.7 million, about the cost of producing a major movie. That pays to keep the meetings running, covering travel, scientific support and workshops, especially for developing countries.
Next year’s budget remains uncertain, but a concerted push by nations to increase funding at the upcoming climate summit in Turkey could be effective, history shows. In 1999, at COP5, an urgent funding appeal in the meeting’s final decision document helped the IPCC maintain momentum for its third and fourth cycles of updated climate reports.
Repeated reminders from the annual climate COPs helped sustain funding through the early 2010s, leading up to the landmark Fifth Assessment Report that is the scientific basis of the 2015 Paris Agreement, which aims to limit human-caused warming as close to 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit (1.5C) as possible.
Scientists Speak
The United States has, at times, contributed as much as one-third of the IPCC’s annual budget. The Trump administration’s withdrawal of funding over the last two years, along with the U.S. government’s withdrawal from the panel, likely contributed to stalling the IPCC process, said Bob Kopp, a climate scientist and professor at Rutgers University, who signed the Oct. 19 letter and has worked on several of the panel’s reports.
Despite the loss of federal support, the United States still has a significant scientific presence in the current assessment cycle, Kopp said. The U.S. Academic Alliance for the IPCC was formed in 2025 by the American Geophysical Union, bringing together colleges and universities to help ensure continued U.S. scientist participation without federal support. He said the U.S. has the largest percentage of contributing authors of any country, about 7.5 percent, and that the alliance nominated more authors for the current cycle than the U.S. government did for the previous one.
“I’m very pleased that civil society in the U.S. has managed to fill some of this gap,” he said. “But we can also see from what’s happening among the governments and the IPCC budget that there’s only so much civil society can do on its own.”

Key IPCC reports are scheduled to track whether countries are living up to what they promised in the Paris Agreement, said Carl Schleussner, a climate scientist with Climate Analytics and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis. Without a timeline for those reports, scientists can’t plan their IPCC-related work schedule, he said.
The delay in the IPCC’s process reflects a range of complex factors, against a backdrop of deteriorating international cooperation. Among them are concerns raised by a group known as the Like-Minded Developing Countries, including India and China. They are questioning whether the panel’s scenarios fairly represent the range of possible climate pathways for all countries, according to reports by observers with the International Institute for Sustainable Development’s Earth Negotiations Bulletin.
Weaponized Science?
Davide Faranda, another IPCC author who signed the letter, said he’s concerned that a breakdown of international collaboration could lead to climate information being weaponized.
If the IPCC fails to provide that timely, widely available knowledge, major powers like the United States or Russia could try to keep climate assessments private to gain strategic advantages through knowledge of climate impacts on agriculture, natural resources, national security and other sectors, he said.
“I think that everyone is aware that climate change now is hitting the entire world like a hammer … and the consequences are here,” said Faranda, who studies climate extremes at the French National Center for Scientific Research in Paris. “Having a report that is transparent and accepted worldwide is important.”
The delays in IPCC decision-making may also reflect the broader redistribution of power in a volatile world. He said the process “should respect that there are new equilibria” emerging.
“We cannot have the deliberations driven only again by European and British and American scientists,” he said. “We have to make it more inclusive. We have to respect the fact that there are countries that are developing fast, and they need to have a stronger voice also in the IPCC.”
The panel’s overall role may be shifting, added Mike Hulme, a professor of human geography at the University of Cambridge who has studied the IPCC.
In the late 1980s and early 1990s, the IPCC mission was clear, he said: detect if the climate is changing and whether humans are causing the warming. The panel answered those straightforward scientific questions by the mid-1990s. After that, things became more complicated.
The climate crisis, he said, raises deep and fundamental questions about the trajectory of human development on the planet. Today, the IPCC grapples with questions that have significant political implications, including how to address global warming through mitigation, adaptation, geoengineering and carbon removal.
The resulting political tension can slow the IPCC’s work, Hulme said. That tension, he added, is also reflected in questions about the coal-producing status of the current two COP31 host countries, Turkey and Australia, and of previous hosts with economies heavily dependent on fossil fuels.
“These political things are very much in the foreground right now,” Hulme said. “The idea that the IPCC can somehow run through that fire with some sort of fireproof clothing on is a non-starter.”

We do not charge a subscription fee, lock our news behind a paywall, or clutter our website with ads. We make our news on climate and the environment freely available to you and anyone who wants it.
That’s not all. We also share our news for free with scores of other media organizations around the country. Many of them can’t afford to do environmental journalism of their own. We’ve built bureaus from coast to coast to report local stories, collaborate with local newsrooms and co-publish articles so that this vital work is shared as widely as possible.
Two of us launched ICN in 2007. Six years later we earned a Pulitzer Prize for National Reporting, and now we run the oldest and largest dedicated climate newsroom in the nation. NASA announced a suite of awards and mission updates on Saturday to expand the agency’s Moon Base exploration, science, and infrastructure capabilities. The investments will advance commercial robotic deliveries, a nuclear-powered rover named PROMISE, launch and orbital transfer services, and surface infrastructure as the agency works with American industry to establish a sustained presence on the Moon’s South Pole.
The agency shared the news at the MAX POWER aerospace expo and air show at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.
“We are building the Moon Base mission by mission,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “Today’s announcements expand nearly every part of that campaign, using the playbook that carried NASA through its greatest eras: fly often, learn, apply those lessons, and get more better and more capable with every mission. When our astronauts return to the Moon, they will arrive with the first elements of the Moon Base already waiting for them on the surface.”
“In the eight months since Ignition, we’ve made incredible strides in accomplishing the near impossible: establishing a permanent outpost on the lunar surface,” said Carlos García-Galán, manager, Moon Base Program. “We’ve consolidated numerous efforts into a streamlined program, evolving our human exploration architecture into an iterative and sustained campaign for Moon Base technology development and implementation. Most importantly, we’ve taken action, awarding new contracts and forging new partnerships to accelerate development.”
Moon Base cargo landers
To strengthen the cargo lander network needed to support the Moon Base, NASA selected eight companies for the next phase of its CLPS (Commercial Lunar Payload Services) initiative. The companies are eligible to compete for future lunar surface delivery missions under the new CLPS 2 contract:
- Blue Origin
- Firefly Aerospace
- Intuitive Machines
- ispace-U.S.
- Lockheed Martin Space
- Northrop Grumman Space Systems
- SpaceX
- Voyager Technologies
Under the CLPS 2 framework, the companies will provide lunar delivery services, including managing, building, and operating landers that transport NASA science, technology, and infrastructure payloads to the Moon.
The CLPS 2 framework is a 10-year, multiple-award, indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity master contract with a combined maximum value of $10 billion. NASA increased the value of the current CLPS 1.0 contract from $2.6 billion to $4.2 billion to support initial Phase One Moon Base objectives. The original CLPS contract will remain in place through November 2028, with an additional five-year period to complete awarded lunar deliveries through November 2033.
Nuclear-powered Moon rover
NASA also announced it is moving forward with development of PROMISE (Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration). Carrying science instruments and technology demonstrations, the six-wheeled rover will land at the Moon’s South Pole to characterize the surface and subsurface, assess resource potential, and provide data to enable landing site selection, as well as future infrastructure and exploration activities. The nuclear-powered rover can operate during long lunar nights and within permanently shadowed regions thought to harbor ice, which is crucial for a sustained human presence on the Moon.
The agency’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, a division of Caltech, will manage the mission and build the rover from a combination of spare flight components and engineering test models for NASA’s Curiosity and Perseverance Mars rovers. Using proven hardware, software, and Mars rover operation approaches significantly reduces cost and enables integration and testing of the complex PROMISE rover on a shorter timeline. NASA has assessed the compatibility of the hardware with the lunar environment and determined it can tolerate the harsh conditions found near the Moon’s South Pole.
The PROMISE rover will carry a drill to extract regolith, or lunar dust, to characterize ice and other resources from approximately 3 feet (1 meter) below the surface, spectrometers for analyzing the chemical composition of surface material, temperature and radiation sensors, and visible-light cameras. It will demonstrate a next-generation, radiation-tolerant computing system, NASA’s High Performance Spaceflight Computing, and advanced autonomy sensors and algorithms. NASA is targeting late 2028 to launch PROMISE and planning an 18-month mission for the rover.
NASA awarded Blue Origin a $94 million base contract, with an option period worth an additional $140 million based on performance to deliver PROMISE to the lunar South Pole. The award expands the task order awarded in May 2026 to deliver two lunar terrain vehicles to the Moon. Blue Origin will use its Mark 1 lander to deliver and deploy the rover as part of the Moon Base’s first phase.
Launch, transportation awards
Delivering Moon Base infrastructure will require a robust transportation network between Earth and the Moon. Orbital Transfer Vehicles (OTVs) act like long-distance freight trucks, carrying large loads across space. Lunar landers handle the final delivery, bringing supplies, equipment, and infrastructure safely down to the Moon’s surface.
To demonstrate those capabilities, NASA awarded six task orders as part of the agency’s Venture-Class Acquisition of Dedicated and Rideshare (VADR) launch services contract. The awards were given to Arrow Science and Technology, Blue Origin, and Impulse Space to integrate and transport Moon Base cargo.
Three mission types will allow NASA flexibility to fly science and technology demonstrations when they are ready.
The first will include missions to reduce risks of future long-term human spaceflight for lunar exploration. The missions will verify that communication and navigation methods work properly during the journey from Earth orbit to the Moon, and OTV capability to support delivery of a CLPS lunar lander to a desired orbit. This mission type will deliver the CAPSTONE 02 spacecraft to deep space to test proximity maneuvers, navigation, and communications around the Moon.
The second category of missions will prepare the lunar South Pole for human exploration by sending a group of highly mobile drones to survey the surface before astronauts arrive, enabling safer, more informed human missions while demonstrating advanced robotic capabilities. Such missions will include the agency’s MoonFall drones, designed to scout areas beyond the reach of traditional rovers, as well as delivery of additional Moon Base assets necessary to support Phase One objectives.
To reduce risk for future missions, the third mission type will test navigation technologies and demonstrate operations in multiple cislunar orbits, between Earth and the Moon. This mission type will demonstrate commercial orbital transfer capabilities intended to increase the amount of cargo that future landers can deliver to the lunar surface.
The task orders have a value of approximately $1.3 billion combined and fall under the 10-year VADR indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract, which has a maximum total value of $5 billion across all contracts. The VADR contracts are managed by NASA’s Launch Services Program Office at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center as part of the agency’s Commercial Access to Space Program. By procuring multiple launch and in-space transportation services together, NASA provides industry with a more predictable set of mission opportunities while gaining access to a broader range of commercial capabilities for future lunar exploration.
Some missions will launch aboard Blue Origin’s New Glenn, Relativity Space’s Terran R, and SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rockets. In-space transportation spacecraft for these missions will be provided by Blue Origin, Firefly Aerospace, Impulse Space, and Quantum Space.
Complementing those in-space transportation demonstrations, NASA selected SpaceX for the Cislunar Communications Deployment Demonstration under an existing lunar logistics contract. Through a Specialized Delivery Mission task order, SpaceX will launch communications satellites aboard a Starship to cislunar space in 2028. The demonstration will help inform the development of future lunar communications networks that keep astronauts, mission controllers, and the Moon Base connected.
Lunar architecture, infrastructure
To extend infrastructure capabilities on the lunar surface, NASA plans to purchase commercial components for a Mini-Communications and Solar Tower (miniCAST), including solar arrays, batteries, and wireless power-transfer hardware. The agency awarded Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin company, for energy storage capability, Redwire for power generation, and Yank Technologies, Inc., for wireless power transfer in support of miniCAST.
The miniCAST will combine power and communications capabilities to support future Moon Base activities. Engineers at NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, will assemble and test the systems before they are delivered to the lunar surface.
NASA expects work to begin within months, and the initial effort will involve components rather than a major integrated system. The agency also plans a separate solicitation for fully integrated power systems, which is anticipated in early 2027.
NASA intends to release a directed call under its Next Space Technologies for Exploration Partnerships, or NextSTEP-3 B, solicitation to help close architecture-driven, high-priority data gaps for Moon Base development. The effort will help NASA gather information it needs to plan future missions, reduce risk, and support technologies and infrastructure for sustained operations on the Moon’s South Pole. The work could include small spacecraft missions, payloads on future Moon Base flights, or the purchase of data collected by commercial partners.
As part of a Golden Age of innovation and exploration, NASA will send Artemis astronauts on increasingly difficult missions to the lunar South Pole to explore more of the Moon than ever before. In addition to providing economic benefits and advancing scientific discovery through its Moon missions, NASA will establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface and build on this foundation for the first crewed mission to Mars.

depeches.titre: « Il faut que j'aille à Stockholm pour me retirer sur place sinon je prends une grosse amende » : après sa demi-finale à Paris, Van Assche contraint d'aller en Suède pour déclarer forfait
depeches.resume: Initialement dans le tableau de l'ATP 250 de Stockholm qui a commencé dimanche, Luca Van Assche, demi-finaliste du Rolex Paris Masters, s'est retiré. Mais il a avoué à RMC qu'il devait se rendre en Suède pour se retirer sur place, sous peine d'écoper d'une amende.

depeches.titre: La France remporte la Coupe Davis juniors pour la première fois depuis 21 ans
depeches.resume: L'équipe de France, composée de Benoît Geldof, Joseph Phitoussi et Pablo Pradat, a remporté dimanche la Coupe Davis juniors, la Coupe du monde des U16, aux dépens de la République tchèque, au Caire (Égypte). Une première depuis 2005.

depeches.titre: Linda Noskova lance les Finales WTA avec un succès autoritaire contre Marta Kostyuk
depeches.resume: Linda Noskova a remporté ce dimanche le premier match des Finales WTA face à Marta Kostyuk (6-2, 6-4), qui a remplacé au pied levé Elena Rybakina, forfait à la veille du tournoi. Les deux joueuses découvraient chacune la compétition.

depeches.titre: Les temps forts de la victoire de Carlos Alcaraz face à Ben Sheltonen finale du Rolex Paris Masters
Monfils, les dessous d'une décision qui a pris tout le monde à contre-pied
C'était pourtant l'arme fatale de Ben Shelton : comment Carlos Alcaraz a neutralisé le service de l'Américain en finale du Rolex Paris Masters
depeches.resume: Sacré au Rolex Paris Masters pour la première fois dimanche (7-6 [5], 7-5), Carlos Alcaraz a construit son succès sur sa qualité de retour et sa capacité à dompter la première balle de service de Ben Shelton, pourtant l'un des principaux atouts de l'Américain.

depeches.titre: Après son sacre au Rolex Paris Masters, quels titres manquent au palmarès de Carlos Alcaraz ?
depeches.resume: En remportant dimanche le Masters 1000 de Paris aux dépens de Ben Shelton, Carlos Alcaraz a garni son armoire d'un nouveau trophée différent. À 23 ans, l'Espagnol a quasiment gagné toutes les grandes compétitions.

depeches.titre: Une semaine au show et Alcaraz a fini par briser sa malédiction
Ben Shelton après sa défaite contre Carlos Alcaraz en finale du Rolex Paris Masters : « Tout se joue sur des petits détails »
depeches.resume: Ben Shelton, battu par Carlos Alcaraz en finale du Rolex Paris Masters dimanche (7-6 [5], 7-5), était satisfait de son état d'esprit et de son adaptation sur surface rapide, loin d'être sa préférée...

depeches.titre: Carlos Alcaraz après sa victoire au Rolex Paris Masters : « Mentalement, j'ai franchi un cap »
depeches.resume: Le déclic lors du match face à Taylor Fritz, les efforts pour contrôler ses émotions depuis le premier point du tournoi, Carlos Alcaraz livre les secrets qui lui ont permis de remporter son premier Rolex Paris Masters.

depeches.titre: La délivrance à 27 ans : Matteo Martineau remporte son premier Challenger en Italie et pourra disputer les qualifications de l'Open d'Australie
depeches.resume: Alors qu'il s'était incliné à cinq reprises en finale, Matteo Martineau a remporté, à 27 ans, son tout premier titre en Challenger à Tarante (Italie) aux dépens du Suisse Kilian Feldbausch (6-3, 6-2) dimanche. Un trophée qui va lui permettre de s'approcher de nouveau du top 200 et de disputer les qu

depeches.titre: Carlos Alcaraz domine Ben Shelton en finale du Rolex Paris Masters et remporte son premier Masters 1000 à Paris
depeches.resume: Carlos Alcaraz à nouveau roi dans la Ville Lumière. L'Espagnol a battu ce dimanche Ben Shelton en finale du Rolex Paris Masters en deux manches (7-6 [5], 7-5). Il s'agit de son premier Masters 1000 dans la capitale française.

depeches.titre: Quentin Halys et Pierre-Hugues Herbert après leur victoire en double au Rolex Paris Masters : « Le but, c'était d'aller chercher un gros titre »
depeches.resume: Quentin Halys et Pierre-Hugues Herbert, associés pour la victoire en double au Rolex Paris Masters dimanche, ont validé le concept d'une association née en fin de saison dernière.

depeches.titre: Fin de saison pour Luca Van Assche qui renonce au tournoi de Stockholm
depeches.resume: Luca Van Assche a décidé de mettre fin à sa saison après sa demi-finale au Rolex Paris Masters samedi (perdue 5-7, 6-3, 6-4 contre Ben Shelton). Il ne se rendra pas à Stockholm pour le dernier tournoi de l'année.

depeches.titre: Quentin Halys et Pierre-Hugues Herbert titrés en double du Rolex Paris Masters
depeches.resume: Les Français Quentin Halys et Pierre-Hugues Herbert ont remporté, ce dimanche à la Plenitude Arena, la finale du double du Rolex Paris Masters. Les Tricolores se sont offert la paire Neal Skupski et Christian Harrison au super tie-break (7-6 [3], 6-7 [4], 10-8).

depeches.titre: Cédric Pioline, directeur du Rolex Paris Masters : « Les fans se sont approprié le lieu »
depeches.resume: Pour sa deuxième année à la Plenitude Arena, Cédric Pioline tire un bilan positif du Rolex Paris Masters. Il estime que le déménagement a été digéré par les fans et revient sur différents points qui ont pu animer la semaine.

depeches.titre: Paris attend son nouveau vainqueur
Entre Carlos Alcaraz et Ben Shelton, le Rolex Paris Masters attend son nouveau vainqueur
depeches.resume: Qu'il s'agisse de Carlos Alcaraz ou de Ben Shelton, le Rolex Paris Masters fêtera un vainqueur inédit au terme de sa 40e finale.

depeches.titre: « Il m'a dit qu'il était très heureux pour moi » : Ben Shelton révèle avoir prévenu Alcaraz qu'il avait embauché Ferrero avant l'officialisation
depeches.resume: Après sa qualification pour la finale du Rolex Paris Masters aux dépens de Luca Van Assche samedi, Ben Shelton a avoué au micro de Tennis Channel qu'il avait informé Carlos Alcaraz de sa collaboration à venir avec Juan Carlos Ferrero avant que l'officialisation ne soit faite.

depeches.titre: Les temps forts du quart de finale du Rolex Paris Masters entre Luca Van Assche et Ben Shelton
Les temps forts du quart de finale du Rolex Paris Masters entre Carlos Alcaraz et Taylor Fritz

Quentin Halys et Pierre-Hugues Herbert se paient les numéros 1 mondiaux et se qualifient pour la finale du double au Rolex Paris Masters
depeches.resume: Quentin Halys et Pierre-Hugues Herbert se sont qualifiés pour la finale du double au Rolex Paris Masters en s'offrant samedi soir les numéros 1 mondiaux de la spécialité, le Finlandais Harri Heliovaara et le Britannique Henry Patten (6-4, 7-6 [3]). La paire française visera le titre dimanche à parti

depeches.titre: « Mon corps n'est pas prêt à disputer cette compétition » : la numéro 1 mondiale Elena Rybakina déclare forfait pour les Finales WTA
depeches.resume: Alors qu'elle devait débuter la compétition dimanche face à Linda Noskova, la numéro 1 mondiale Elena Rybakina a annoncé, samedi, qu'elle déclarait forfait pour les Finales WTA, ne s'estimant pas prête. La Kazakhstanaise est remplacée par Marta Kostyuk.

depeches.titre: David Ferrer sera l'entraîneur de Casper Ruud la saison prochaine
depeches.resume: Selon une information d'Eurosport Espagne que nous sommes en mesure de confirmer, David Ferrer, qui va quitter son poste de capitaine de l'équipe d'Espagne de Coupe Davis à la fin de l'année, va entraîner à partir de la saison prochaine le Norvégien Casper Ruud.

depeches.titre: Comment Luca Van Assche a dilapidé son break d'avance dans le troisième set et perdu le fil face à Ben Shelton au Rolex Paris Masters
depeches.resume: Luca Van Assche, qui menait 3-1 dans le troisième set de sa demi-finale du Rolex Paris Masters face à Ben Shelton samedi, a fini par s'incliner (7-5, 3-6, 6-4) face à l'Américain. Des fautes directes ont condamné le Français de 22 ans lors du jeu pour confirmer son break.

depeches.titre: Trop fort pour Casper Ruud, Carlos Alcaraz va disputer sa première finale face à Ben Shelton au Rolex Paris Masters
depeches.resume: Sans trembler, Carlos Alcaraz a dominé un Casper Ruud diminué en demi-finales du Rolex Paris Masters (6-4, 6-4), ce samedi. Pour sa première finale au Masters 1000 francilien, l'Espagnol retrouvera Ben Shelton, tombeur de Luca Van Assche.

depeches.titre: Luca Van Assche après sa défaite en demi-finales du Rolex Paris Masters face à Ben Shelton : « Je n'ai pas de regrets, je me suis donné à fond »
depeches.resume: Battu en demi-finales du Rolex Paris Masters ce samedi après-midi par Ben Shelton (5-7, 6-3, 6-4), Luca Van Assche assure ne pas avoir de regrets malgré un break d'avance dans le troisième set, et espère pouvoir capitaliser sur sa belle semaine à Nanterre.

depeches.titre: Gilles Simon sur la nomination de Gaël Monfils comme capitaine de l'équipe de France de Coupe Davis : « Ça lui tenait à coeur, plus que ce que vous pouvez imaginer »
depeches.resume: Gilles Moretton, président de la FFT, et Gilles Simon, directeur de la haute performance, ont expliqué samedi, en marge du Rolex Paris Masters, les raisons qui ont mené au choix de nommer Gaël Monfils capitaine de l'équipe de France de Coupe Davis.

depeches.titre: Alcaraz, sacré boucan et show renversant
Battu en trois sets par Ben Shelton, Luca Van Assche s'arrête en demi-finales du Rolex Paris Masters
depeches.resume: Malgré un break d'avance dans le troisième set, Luca Van Assche a vu son beau parcours au Rolex Paris Masters s'arrêter en demi-finales ce samedi après-midi face à Ben Shelton (5-7, 6-3, 6-4). L'Américain, 4e mondial et finaliste du dernier US Open, affrontera Carlos Alcaraz (3e)  dimanche pour le t
